The Objective Ledger: The whole book, the short version.
By Christian. Spread Love & Acceptance.

This edition: October 2026. Made from the chapters at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book, where they are kept up to date.

Free to read and share. You may print, copy and share this book for personal use and for non-commercial teaching, as long as you credit “The Objective Ledger, spreadloveandacceptance.com” and don’t change it or sell it.

Not therapy. This book is general education about people and relationships. It is not a diagnosis, treatment or a replacement for help from a doctor, counsellor or other trained professional, and it can’t know your situation.

If you are not safe. If you feel afraid of someone you live with, or someone controls your money, phone or movements, that is not a problem to fix with a worksheet. spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety lists free, private help. If you are in danger now, call your local emergency number.

The examples are made up. The people in the scenes and examples are invented, built from common patterns. None of them is a real person or a testimonial.

Research mentioned in the chapters is listed, with links, in the research notes at the back and at spreadloveandacceptance.com/research.

Set in Lora, Fraunces and IBM Plex Mono.

If you need help now

If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, or someone is in danger right now, call your local emergency number: 999 in the UK, 112 or 999 in Ireland, 911 in the US and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand.

If you are struggling, or worried about someone else, you can talk to a trained person now. These lines are free, private and open day and night. You don’t have to be sure it is a crisis to call or text.

Where you areCall or text
United StatesCall or text 988 (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), or chat at 988lifeline.org. You can also text HOME to 741741 (Crisis Text Line).
United KingdomCall Samaritans free on 116 123. Or text SHOUT to 85258 (Shout, a free text line).
IrelandCall Samaritans free on 116 123.
CanadaCall or text 9-8-8 (the Suicide Crisis Helpline), in English or French.
AustraliaCall Lifeline on 13 11 14, or text 0477 13 11 14.
New ZealandCall or text 1737 (Need to talk?).
Anywhere elsefindahelpline.com lists free helplines in many countries, by phone, text and chat.

For children and young people

UKChildline, 0800 1111 (free, for anyone under 19)
IrelandChildline, 1800 66 66 66 (free, for anyone up to 18)
CanadaKids Help Phone, 1-800-668-6868, or text CONNECT to 686868
AustraliaKids Helpline, 1800 55 1800 (ages 5 to 25)
New ZealandYouthline, 0800 376 633, or text 234
US988 is for every age.

If you’re worried about someone

Ask them plainly: “Are you thinking about ending your life?” Studies have found that asking does not put the idea in someone’s head, and talking about it may even ease it. Listen, stay with them if you can, and call or text one of the lines above together. Part Three, Chapter 12, page 366 says more about helping someone in a crisis, and Chapter 16, page 442 about worry, low mood and when to get help.

This book is general education, not a crisis service. The website’s tools keep what you type on your own device, so nobody there can see it or reply to it. The numbers were checked in October 2026. Numbers can change; findahelpline.com keeps an up-to-date list.

zqhowqz

How to use this book

This is a book about seeing what is really going on, in yourself and between people, without blaming anyone, and then changing one small thing. This copy holds 26 chapters in three parts, in the short version. There is no wrong way in.

The parts

  • Part One: Self-discovery. Where you came from, who you are now and who you are becoming. You can read all of it on your own.
  • Part Two: Between us. One idea per chapter about sharing a life, a home or work with someone, each with a worksheet that puts it to use.
  • Part Three: Understanding people. How feelings, stress, trust, change, grief, groups and love work, for anyone, in any kind of relationship.

Two sizes of every chapter

Every chapter comes in a short version (about 10 to 15 minutes) and a full version with the research, more examples and more to try. This is the short version. The full version is free at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book.

Read in order, or by need

Read it front to back like any book, or start with the chapter that fits what is going on. Each chapter ends with What to remember, This connects to (the chapters that explain it or put it to use, with page numbers) and Put it to use, with codes you can scan for the matching tool.

In every chapter

  • A short scene: a made-up moment from everyday life.
  • Words you could use: sentences to say out loud.
  • Try this: one small thing to do this week.
  • Common mix-ups: easy mistakes, and what is closer to true.

The site, the program and Professor Puddles

The book has a free website with the workpapers (pages you fill in) and tools (helpers you use) that the chapters mention; the next page explains both. Nothing you type there leaves your device, and there is no account. The six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01) puts Part Two to work a week at a time, and the self path does the same for Part One. Professor Puddles, the site’s friendly guide, answers questions about the book’s ideas.

Go gently

Some chapters touch hard things: grief, shame, anger, worry, trauma. Skip anything that isn’t right for today. Nothing here is a test, and nothing needs to be done all at once.

Workpapers, tools and three friends

Workpaper WP-03 Workpapers: pages you fill in

A workpaper is a page you fill in, on your own or together: a one-week log, a list of who owns which job, a short check. Each one has a number, like WP-03, and it is always called a workpaper, for example “Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job”. The blank workpapers are also at the back of this book, one page each, to copy.

Tool Tools: helpers you use on the site

A tool is an interactive helper on the website: a quiz, a calm-down timer, a card maker, or the Chat analyzer that reads a message with you. You use it and it gives you something back. It is always called a tool, for example “Tool: Chat analyzer”.

The book keeps the two apart: a workpaper and a tool never share a list. Both are free, need no account, and what you type stays on your device.

Three friends who give hints

  • Professor Puddles, the site’s cheerful raindrop professor, gives most of the hints: a thought to take with you, and the workpaper or tool that fits.
  • Tidbit, the quick, curious pup with the big smile and the collar, bounds in now and then with a playful tip.
  • Sugarfoot, the steady, gentle pup with the long soft ears and the best hugs, turns up with a calm, slow tip.

They keep to the lighter pages. Where a chapter talks about crisis, deep grief or being hurt, the pages stay quiet and plain.

zqhandedqz

If someone handed you this book

Maybe it was left on your side of the bed with a page turned down. Maybe someone said, “Could you just read this bit?” Either way, you didn’t choose it. Fair enough. Here is the short version, written for you.

This isn’t a case against you

The book starts from something researchers have found again and again: when two people each estimate their share of the housework, the two answers usually add up to more than 100%. Nobody is lying. You see every minute of your own effort and only some of theirs, and so do they (Chapter II, page 110). So the book never asks who the bad guy is. Its numbers score the setup, never a person.

What’s in it for you

  • Fewer repeat arguments about the same jobs.
  • Jobs that are clearly yours, so nobody needs to remind you about them.
  • Credit for what you already do. Your jobs go on the list too: the car, the bins, the late-night lifts, the things you fix.
  • A say in what “fair” means in your house. It isn’t always 50/50 (Chapter IV, page 151).

It doesn’t ask for therapy talk, and you never fill anything in about the other person. You can say no.

A first week: three small things

  1. Log your own week. Rough minutes on “Who did what”, including the thinking part: booking, remembering, planning. Ten minutes in all. Only yours, never theirs.
  2. Ask one question, and just listen. “What’s the one job you’d most like to stop thinking about?” Don’t defend or count. Write the answer down.
  3. Take over that job, the whole of it, including the noticing (below).

Words to open the talk

“I read the bit you gave me. I don’t agree with all of it, but I get the point about the stuff nobody sees.”
“I’d rather own a couple of things properly than ‘help’ with everything. Which one would you most like off your mind?”
“Give me a week to see what I actually do. Then let’s look together.”

Best left out, for now: “Just tell me what to do” (it hands the thinking straight back), “You should have asked” and, in the first five minutes, “I do loads too.” That may be true. Save it for when you both have your logs.

Taking over a whole job, noticing included

Every job has a part you can see (doing it) and parts you can’t: noticing it needs doing, remembering, planning and checking it got done (the Preface, page 74). Taking a job over means all of it.

  1. Pick one job that repeats: the children’s clothes and shoes, the bins, the car, school forms, the dentist.
  2. Get the handover once. What it involves, when it’s due, where things are, who to call. Ask your questions now, not every week.
  3. Move the remembering out of their head. A phone reminder, the calendar, a list on the fridge: anywhere but the other person.
  4. Do it start to finish for a month without being reminded. If you need reminding, fix your reminder, not the relationship.
  5. Do it your way. If the result is fine, the method is yours. Their part is to let it be done differently.
  6. Ask for a backstop if you like: someone who notices a slip and says so once, kindly. A backstop isn’t a supervisor (Chapter II, page 110).

A made-up example. Hester has always looked after the children’s clothes: spotting toes at the end of shoes, school sizes, swimming kit, passing on what’s outgrown. Wilf takes it over. Hester writes the handover note: sizes, the shop, which drawer holds the next size up. Wilf sets a reminder for the first Sunday of each month: “Shoes, uniform, kit.” In week two he misses the PE kit for a school trip. Hester says once, “The trip kit is Thursday,” and he adds “school letters” to his Sunday check. A month in, Hester says the biggest change is that she no longer thinks about shoes at eleven at night.

If you think it’s already fair

Log your week anyway. If it comes out even, that is useful to know, and the book will say so: a fair score doesn’t silence anyone, and a low one doesn’t blame anyone. And if this book feels like the wrong place to start, Find it fast, page 9 lists other ways in.

Part One · Then

Know yourself: then, where your lens came from

Why you expect what you expect, and how the rules you picked up growing up still make small decisions for you today.

In this chapter

  1. You’re not one thing
  2. Your lens came from somewhere
  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question
  4. When something happened matters
  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts
  6. An old rule can read other people for you
  7. Write down the rulebook from home
  8. You get to choose which rules to keep
  9. The past isn’t yours to change. What you carry forward is
  10. The ideas, one at a time
  11. You, in all your relationships
  12. Inside you, and between you
  13. In the individual program
  14. The fields behind this part
  15. In real life
  16. Common mix-ups

This is where the book begins. Part One (Then, Now and Next) is about you. Part Two (a Preface and Chapters I to V) is about the people you share a life with. Part Three (Chapters 1 to 17) is about how people work. Some printed copies hold only one or two of the parts; every chapter is free to read at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book, and the book at a glance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-start-here) there gives a one-minute tour of the whole thing.

In short:

  • You’re not one thing. A reaction comes from your wiring (it stays), the patterns life taught you (they can soften) and today’s conditions (they pass). This part is about the patterns.
  • Your lens came from somewhere: home, school, culture, money and what you lived through. Each stage of growing up asked its own question.
  • Some old rules were learned without all the facts, and they can read other people for you: “Whoever notices, does it.”
  • Write down the rulebook from home, then choose which rules to keep.
  • The past isn’t yours to change. What you carry forward is.

The big ideas: This part mostly teaches “Read your state first” and “Notice the quiet incentives”, with help from “See the whole load” and “Fix the setup, not the person”. What are the five big ideas? (They are five plain ideas the whole program is built on.)

Sunday, 10:15am

Your partner is still in bed and the kitchen is a mess. Before you’ve had a single thought, you feel it: “Of course. It’s always me.” Nobody said that. But in the house you grew up in, whoever noticed the mess cleaned it. That old rule just made a decision for you.

Or, living alone: Since his wife died, Ray’s house is quiet and nobody will see the dishes. He still can’t sit down until every one is done. Nobody is watching. An old rule from the home he grew up in still is.

  1. You’re not one thing.

    A reaction usually comes from three places at once: how you’re built (your wiring, which stays), what life taught you (patterns, many of which can soften) and what kind of day you’re having (conditions, which pass). This part is about the middle one, the patterns life taught you. Now (page 39) looks at the other two.

    Dig deeper: the three layers

  2. Your lens came from somewhere.

    Family, school, friends, culture, money at home and what you watched all taught you what to expect: of yourself, of other people, and of how a “good” partner, parent or friend behaves. By adulthood your lens doesn’t feel like a lens. It feels like simply seeing. Where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) walks through it, and you can read one section and stop.

    Dig deeper: the lens idea

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: the rules from home aren’t good or bad, they’re just yours to have a good sniff at. A fun first look is how you like to talk.

    Tool: Communication style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question.

    Is the world safe? Can I do it myself? Am I capable? Where do I belong? Can I be close without losing myself? And later in life: What am I building? Has my life meant something? The ages are rough and people move at their own pace. The answers you landed on can become understandings you keep using as an adult.

    Dig deeper: the stages

  4. When something happened matters.

    An experience that touches the question you were answering at the time tends to go deeper. A move at 4 is mostly about routines. A move at 14, in the middle of “Where do I belong?”, can leave a longer feeling of being the outsider. Deeper isn’t permanent, though: people keep learning all their lives.

    Dig deeper: why timing matters

  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts.

    “I’m only okay when I’m useful.” “My needs are a burden.” “Mistakes mean I’m bad.” A child often can’t know what was going on for the grown-ups. They only know how it felt. As an adult, you’re allowed to look again with the full picture. Looking again doesn’t mean deciding it was all fine, because some things really were not okay.

    Dig deeper: old answers and fairer readings

  6. An old rule can read other people for you.

    If silence at home meant anger, a partner’s quiet evening can feel like trouble is coming. And an expectation nobody said out loud can’t be agreed to, so the other person can only miss it: “If you loved me, you’d just know.” “Whoever notices, does it.” Each is somebody’s family rule, not a law of nature. Ask before you conclude: “When you went quiet, what was going on for you?”

    Dig deeper: rules that read others

    Professor Puddles

    When an old rule jumps in before you’ve had a chance to think, you don’t have to argue with it. Write it down, and look at it again on a calm day.

    Tool: Where a reaction comes from spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up

  7. Write down the rulebook from home.

    Finish these six lines the way your childhood home would have: “In my family, love looked like…” “When someone was upset, we…” “The jobs were split like this…” “Resting was okay when…” “Asking for help meant…” “The unforgivable thing was…” The rulebook page has room to write them. Nothing is saved except on your own device.

    Dig deeper: the six rulebook lines

  8. You get to choose which rules to keep.

    For each line, ask: do I still want this rule? When a reaction feels bigger than the moment, try the one-minute lens check once you’ve settled: Where did I learn this? How old does this feel? Is it true here, with this person, now? What would the adult me choose? Later, you can swap rulebooks with someone you trust and choose shared rules on purpose.

    Dig deeper: the lens check, and choosing together

  9. The past isn’t yours to change. What you carry forward is.

    You couldn’t control the home you grew up in, what other people did, or what you learned before you had all the facts. What is in your hands now is smaller, and stronger: which old rules you keep, how you treat yourself about them, and where you spend your energy today. That includes people. Give your time and care where they’re met with care, and let one-sided effort shrink back to what feels fair. Matching energy with energy isn’t cold. It protects what you have, so you still have something to give.

    Dig deeper: your part, then and now

The ideas, one at a time

Each idea above again, with a real-life example, words you could use and one small step. Read one and stop if you like.

1. You’re not one thing

For example: A grandmother snaps when her grown-up son is late for lunch. Part is her wiring (she likes things on time). Part is an old rule (“late means you don’t care”). And part is that she slept badly.

Words you could use: “Some of this is me being tired, and some of it is an old thing. Give me a minute.”

Try this: Next time you react strongly, ask: is this mostly wiring, something I learned, or just today?

2. Your lens came from somewhere

For example: One friend grew up with big birthday parties, the other with quiet ones. A small dinner feels hurtful to one and perfect to the other.

Words you could use: “In my family this was a big deal. What was it like in yours?”

Try this: Pick one thing you think “everyone” does. Ask one person how their family did it.

3. Each stage asks its own question

For example: Someone who moved schools four times as a teen may still feel like the outsider at every new job.

Words you could use: “I think part of me is still asking whether I belong here.”

Try this: Read the questions above and notice which one still feels loud. That’s all.

4. When something happened matters

For example: Two adult siblings remember their parents’ divorce differently. One was six and remembers new routines. The other was fifteen and remembers feeling torn in half. Both are true. See Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts).

Words you could use: “We were different ages when it happened. It makes sense we remember it differently.”

Try this: Think of one big change from growing up. How old were you, and what were you trying to work out?

5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts

For example: A foster carer who learned that “my needs are a burden” finds it hard to ask for respite (a planned break while someone else cares), even when worn out. See Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).

Words you could use: “An old voice says I shouldn’t ask. The adult me thinks asking is fair.”

Try this: Write one old belief about yourself. Under it, write what you’d tell a friend who believed it.

6. An old rule can read other people for you

For example: A housemate leaves without saying goodbye. If quiet meant anger at home, you may think they’re upset. They may just be late for a shift.

Words you could use: “When you went quiet earlier, I wasn’t sure what it meant. Is everything okay?”

Try this: This week, when you catch yourself guessing what someone’s silence means, ask instead.

zqaxselfx1xthenxxpxrulebookqz7. Write down the rulebook from home

For example: Two partners from different faiths both write “holidays belong to my family,” and finally see why December is hard. See Two faiths, one family (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths).

Words you could use: “Here’s a rule I grew up with. I’m not saying it’s right. I just want you to know it’s there.”

Try this: Finish just one of the six lines today. Leave the others for another day.

8. You get to choose which rules to keep

For example: A team leader sees that “mistakes mean I’m bad” makes them hide problems. New rule: “Mistakes are information. We fix them together.”

Words you could use: “I used to think ___. Now I’m choosing ___.”

Try this: Pick one rule from your list and write the version you would like to live by.

9. What you carry forward is yours

For example: Someone living on their own always plans the meetups with one friend, who never asks back. They stop chasing, keep the door open, and see more of the friends who reply. See Always the one reaching out? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends)

Words you could use: “I’d love to see you. Let me know when works for you.”

Try this: Name one relationship where you give far more than comes back, and give a little less this month. (If you are afraid of someone, this isn’t about managing them. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

Tuesday morning

Two people get the same text: “Can we talk tonight?” One thinks, “Good, I like knowing ahead.” The other feels their stomach drop, because in the home they grew up in, “we need to talk” meant trouble. Same words. Two different histories.

You, in all your relationships

Your old rules go wherever you go, starting with how you treat yourself.

  • With yourself: The voice you use after a mistake is often an old one.
  • With a partner, or partners: Who notices, who plans, what quiet means. More than two of you means more than two rulebooks. See More than two partners at home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).
  • With friends: Who reaches out first, and whether asking feels okay. See Friends.
  • With family: Old roles, like the helper or the peacemaker, switch back on at the door. See For grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) and Family rifts.
  • At work: Praised for being useful? You may say yes to everything, then resent it.
  • With housemates: Two rulebooks about mess, noise and guests. See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).
  • On your own: After a breakup, old rules can get louder. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Looking for your own situation? Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists them all.

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Ask whether a feeling is the size of this moment or older. Notice what you were praised or scolded for as a child still pulling on you. Holding an old rule in check is real, hidden effort.
  • Between you and others: A learned rule is part of the setup, not a flaw in anyone. Say your rules out loud, and choose shared ones.

In the individual program

This part goes with Step 3 of the individual program: write the rulebook from the home you grew up in, and choose one rule you’d like to change. You can do every step on your own.

Your next step: Step 3: see where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Where your lens came from · A gentle first week · The whole book on knowing yourself (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-know-yourself)

The fields behind this part

This part draws on 4 of the author’s thirteen fields (the About page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/about) lists them all):

  • Psychology (Read your state first): The lens you learned, the stages of growing up and the old stories we carry.
  • Neurobiology (Read your state first): An old alarm can go off before you’ve had time to think.
  • Philosophy (Notice the quiet incentives): Plato’s cave: shadows that feel like the whole world. A rule you never chose can feel like simply how things are.
  • Behavioural science (Notice the quiet incentives): What got praised or scolded taught you what to do, and repeating something new teaches a new rule.

Two fields, one idea: Psychology + Neurobiology. How you feel and how your nervous system is running are the same moment, seen from two sides. An old alarm is both a feeling and a body state, so noticing it is the first step.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-1-then-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

In real life

  • Partners: “Of course it’s always me.” You grew up in a house where whoever noticed, did. Naming the old rule out loud, on a calm day, turns a fight about dishes into a talk about who owns what.
  • Family: A parent says, “We should talk.” You brace, because quiet meant anger in the house you grew up in. Knowing where the alarm came from, you ask first: “Is this a good talk or a worried one?”
  • Housemates: One housemate grew up where help was never asked for, only given. The other grew up where nothing happened unless you asked. Neither is rude. They are using two rulebooks.
  • Coworkers: Someone who was praised mostly for being useful says yes to everything, then resents it. Seeing the old rule helps them pause before the next yes.

Common mix-ups

  • “Looking back means blaming my family.” It isn’t about blame. Many of the adults who raised us were working with their own lenses too, and if that doesn’t fit your story, you don’t have to make it fit.
  • “If it started in childhood, I’m stuck with it.” Deeper isn’t permanent. Many old patterns soften with awareness, safety and practice, and some leave a lasting sensitivity you learn to carry and explain.
  • “Every big reaction is an old wound.” Often it’s just a full tank. Sort it first: Chapter III (page 132) helps tell leftover stress from this-moment stress.
  • “My rulebook is normal, so theirs is wrong.” Each is somebody’s family rule. Two rulebooks in one home are a setup to talk about, not a verdict on either person.
  • “I have to finish this before I go on.” You don’t. You can read one section and stop, and come back another day.
  • “If they won’t look at their rules, there’s no point looking at mine.” There is. Knowing your own rules changes how you react, even if nobody else ever reads a word of this.

A note on care: This part looks back at growing up. It is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy, and it can’t tell you what anyone has. Not every home felt calm or kind, so take only what is useful. If looking back feels heavy, you can stop and come back another day, or explore it with a qualified professional, if and when you want that. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared.

Try this: Think of one “always” or “never” you felt this week.

Ask: whose voice does this sound like, and how old did I feel?

Then write one sentence the adult you would rather live by, and keep it somewhere you’ll see it.

Where your lens came from → Roots & Wings: find where a trait started → The rulebook from home → Know your own wiring → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself) Next in the book: Now → (page 39)

What to remember

  • You’re not one thing. A reaction comes from your wiring (it stays), the patterns life taught you (they can soften) and today’s conditions (they pass). This part is about the patterns.
  • Your lens came from somewhere: home, school, culture, money and what you lived through. Each stage of growing up asked its own question.
  • Some old rules were learned without all the facts, and they can read other people for you: “Whoever notices, does it.”
  • Write down the rulebook from home, then choose which rules to keep.
  • The past isn’t yours to change. What you carry forward is.

Now

Part One · Now

Know yourself: now, your wiring, your weather and your words

Why the same words can land differently on different days and in different people, and how to understand today’s you well enough to say what helps.

In this chapter

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with
  2. Know how you like to be spoken to
  3. Check your weather before you speak
  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from
  5. Plan what settles you on a calm day
  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands
  7. Being wired differently is not being wrong
  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing
  9. Do your part, and only your part
  10. The ideas, one at a time
  11. You, in all your relationships
  12. Inside you, and between you
  13. In the individual program
  14. The fields behind this part
  15. In real life
  16. Common mix-ups

In short:

  • Today has two layers you can work with: your wiring, which stays (work with it), and today’s conditions, which pass (work around them).
  • Check your state before a hard talk. Weather, the three states, the load and the battery are different words for the same thing: how much room you have today.
  • If a feeling is hard to name, start with the body. That is common, and it has a name: alexithymia.
  • Your needs and limits are information. Plan what settles you on a calm day, and say what helps in one short sentence.
  • Different isn’t wrong. A mix-up between two different minds runs both ways, so both of you adjust a little.

The big ideas: This part mostly teaches “Read your state first” and “Tune how you send and receive”, with help from “See the whole load” and “Fix the setup, not the person”. What are the five big ideas? (They are five plain ideas the whole program is built on.)

Sunday, 7:50pm

A friend asks, “Are you okay?” You say, “Fine.” The truth is you can’t tell whether you’re fine, tired or quietly bothered, and you couldn’t explain it to yourself, let alone to them.

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with.

    Your wiring is the lasting part: your temperament, your pace, your senses, how you take in words. You work with it, by building a setup that suits you. Today’s conditions are the passing part: sleep, hunger, load, the room, the time of day. You work around them: eat first, sleep on it, talk tomorrow. Mixing the two up is where a lot of frustration comes from. (Then (page 22) covered the third layer, the patterns life taught you.)

    Dig deeper: wiring and conditions

    Professor Puddles

    Your wiring stays the same from day to day. Your weather doesn’t. A one-minute check in the morning helps you tell the two apart.

    Tool: How am I right now? A mood and energy check spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  2. Know how you like to be spoken to.

    Your pace, your tone, how much you need spelled out and what silence means to you all change how words land. Wavelength (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) helps you find words for how you think, talk and listen, with a four-letter Wave Code that is a fun description, not a test. The Wiring Card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) puts how you take in words on one page you can share before a hard talk, not during one.

    Dig deeper: your wiring and your Wave Code

  3. Check your weather before you speak.

    Every conversation runs through your own state first. Chapter III (page 132) in Part Two goes deep on the stress tank, so this part only adds the self side: a one-minute reading, on your own, before you decide what a hard moment means. Today’s Weather (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is the quick one, and How much are you carrying? is the fuller one, a short worksheet.

    Dig deeper: reading your state before you speak

  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from.

    Name it (“tight, annoyed, a bit scared”). Then ask: is this the size of the moment, or does it feel older? Which layer is it? And what does it need right now: food, space, a heads-up, reassurance, or a real conversation later? It takes a minute, and it works best once the first wave has passed.

    Dig deeper: a four-step self-check

  5. Plan what settles you on a calm day.

    When you’re wound up is a bad time to work out what helps. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) is a plan you make while calm: what tends to set you off, two calming steps, and one sentence for stepping away that includes when you’ll be back. It is for you, never for the other person.

    Dig deeper: deciding ahead

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: make your calm-down plan on a slow, sunny day, maybe with a cup of tea. It’s much easier than making it in the middle of a storm.

    Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands.

    What helps you, what matters to you and what you have left are facts about you. Said kindly, they let other people plan around you: “A heads-up helps me,” “I can take this one, not that one,” “I’m low today, can we talk tomorrow?” Who did what (Part B) has ready-made kind ways to say no, and Say it so it lands turns a raw reaction into a fact, a feeling and an ask.

    Dig deeper: saying your needs kindly

  7. Being wired differently is not being wrong.

    Some people take in words, noise, change and feelings differently from what most social customs were built around. That is wiring, not a flaw to fix. You can understand it, plan around it and get support for it, if you choose. A mix-up also runs both ways: Wired Differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently) shows how two differently wired people can each misread the other, with nobody at fault.

    Dig deeper: wiring is not a flaw

  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing.

    Three short sentences cover most moments. “This is how I’m wired. It won’t change, but here’s what helps.” “This is an old alarm. I’m working on it, and here’s what helps in the moment.” “Today’s a low-battery day.” You never owe anyone your history. Share the part that helps them help you, as information and not as a list of rules.

    Dig deeper: scripts, and how much to share

  9. Do your part, and only your part.

    Today you control your words, your effort, your rest, your limits and what you ask for. You don’t control someone else’s mood, reply, pace or choices, and trying to manage them drains you fast. So do your side well, then let go of theirs. And match energy with energy: meet warmth with warmth and effort with effort, and when you keep giving far more than comes back, give a little less until it balances. It protects your battery, and a protected battery is what keeps you kind.

    Dig deeper: your circle of control, and matching energy

The ideas, one at a time

Each idea above again, with a real-life example, words you could use and one small step. Read one and stop if you like.

1. Two layers you can work with

For example: A dad who works nights finds the school-run chatter unbearable at 8am. That isn’t who he is. It’s the hour. He swaps to the afternoon pick-up, and the chatter is fun again. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

Words you could use: “It’s not you, it’s the hour. Can we talk after I’ve slept?”

Try this: Write one thing that always bothers you (probably wiring) and one that only bothers you when you’re tired (conditions).

2. How you like to be spoken to

For example: A grandmother loves phone calls. Her grandson loves texts. Each thinks the other is being distant. Once they say how they like to talk, they settle on a Sunday call and texts in between.

Words you could use: “I take things in best when ___. How about you?”

Try this: Finish the sentence “I take things in best when…” and keep it for your Wiring Card (a one-page note on how you like to be spoken to).

3. Check your weather first

For example: A long-distance couple notice their hard calls are always at the end of one partner’s late shift. They move serious talks to weekend mornings. See Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance).

Words you could use: “I’m running on empty tonight. Can we pick this up tomorrow morning?”

Try this: For three mornings, describe your inner weather in one of the three sky words Today’s Weather uses: clear, gusty or fogged in.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxstatexwordsqz

One state, many words. The book and its tools use a few everyday pictures for one thing: how much room you have today. They are different words for the same state, not different things to measure.

  • The three states (Part Three calls them the ladder): calm and connected, revved up, and running on empty.
  • Today’s Weather uses sky words for the same three: clear is calm and connected, gusty is revved up, and fogged in is running on empty. Its pressure (light, building or heavy) is how much you were already carrying.
  • The load, also called the stress tank, is the score from How much are you carrying?, from 0 to 1. Higher means heavier.
  • The battery is the other side of the load: the energy you have left. A heavy load means a low battery.

So “gusty”, “revved up”, “a fairly full tank” and “a low battery” can all describe the same afternoon. Use whichever words suit you.

4. Where is the feeling coming from?

For example: A coworker says, “Quick question?” and your heart races. Name it: jumpy. Older? Yes, an old boss. Layer: a pattern, plus a busy day. Need: a moment to settle.

Words you could use: “Sure. Give me five minutes and I’ll be right with you.”

Try this: Next time a feeling surprises you, do just the first step: name it in two words.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxhardxtoxnameqzWhen feelings are hard to name: For some people, “What are you feeling?” is a hard question most days, not just bad ones. They notice a racing heart or a heavy stomach, but can’t tell if it is worry, anger or hunger. Psychologists call this alexithymia (“no words for feelings”). It is a trait that runs from a little to a lot, not an illness, and it is common, especially in autistic people. The feelings are there; the words come slowly. What helps: start with the body (“tight chest, skipped lunch”), choose between two words (“more tired or more annoyed?”), use the three sky words instead of feeling words, and give it time. “I’ll tell you tomorrow” is a real answer.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxsettleqz5. Plan what settles you

For example: A teenager makes a plan with herself. When a row with her mum heats up, she says, “I need ten minutes in my room, then I’ll come back.” And she comes back.

Words you could use: “I’m too wound up to listen well. I need twenty minutes, then I’ll come back.”

Try this: On a calm day, write your one stepping-away sentence, including when you’ll be back.

6. Needs are information

For example: In a home with three partners, Quinn needs an hour alone after work. Said once, kindly, it becomes part of the plan instead of a mystery. See More than two partners at home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).

Words you could use: “I can do ___. I can’t do ___ this week. Could we ___ instead?”

Try this: Write one need you’ve never said out loud. Practise saying it as a fact, not an apology.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxdifferentqz7. Different isn’t wrong

For example: A woman with ADHD keeps forgetting plans with a friend. Instead of “I’m hopeless,” she says what helps: “If you text me the day before, I’ll be there.” See Neurodivergent relationships (spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

Words you could use: “My brain works a bit differently. Here’s what helps me get it right.”

zqaxselfx2xnowxxdoublexempathyqzA mix-up runs both ways: When an autistic and a non-autistic person misread each other, it is easy to blame the autistic person. The double empathy problem, named by the autistic researcher Damian Milton, is the idea that the gap runs both ways: each person reads the other through their own way of communicating, and each finds the other hard to read. In one study, a story passed along a chain of autistic people kept as much detail as one passed along non-autistic people; mixed chains lost detail faster. So nobody is the broken one. Ask “Where did we lose each other?” and both adjust a little.

Try this: Name one setting where you work best (quiet, written down, early, with music) and give yourself it once this week.

8. Explain, without over-sharing

For example: A man with a long-term illness tells a new friend, “Some days I have less energy. If I cancel, it isn’t about you.” He shares what helps, not his medical history. See When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

Words you could use: “Today’s a low-battery day. It isn’t about you.”

Try this: Pick one of the three short sentences above and say it out loud once, on your own.

9. Your part, and only your part

For example: A grown-up daughter keeps trying to stop her father worrying about her. She can’t. She can send a short “Home safe” text after long drives, then let his worry be his. See For grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children).

Words you could use: “I can’t stop you worrying, but I can text when I’m home.”

Try this: Write one thing you keep trying to control that isn’t yours. Next to it, write one thing that is. (If you are afraid of someone, this isn’t about managing them. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

Friday, 6:40pm

“Surprise! I booked us dinner with my cousins tonight.” They meant it as a gift. You felt your chest tighten and heard yourself say “Great” in a flat voice. Later you wonder: is that just me, is it something from years ago, or am I simply wiped out after this week? Probably a bit of all three.

You, in all your relationships

Your wiring and your weather come with you everywhere, starting with how you treat yourself on a hard day.

  • With yourself: Noticing “I’m low today” before you decide “I’m failing.”
  • With partners: A heads-up, a quiet hour, a better time to talk. Every partner, and every extra partner, has a wiring of their own.
  • With friends and family: How you like to keep in touch, and how much you can give this month. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • At work: An agenda ahead, a written plan, a minute before you answer.
  • With housemates: Noise, light and quiet time. See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).
  • On your own: Building a week that suits how you’re built. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Find your own situation in help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship).

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Check your state and know your wiring before you judge a reaction. Count the hidden effort, like masking (hiding or toning down how you naturally are, to fit in) or holding an old alarm down, as real load.
  • Between you and others: Change the setup, not the person. Tell people what helps, tune how you send and receive, and treat a mismatch as tuning, not a moral failing.

In the individual program

This part goes with Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the individual program: check your battery, get to know your wiring, plan what settles you, and find words for what you feel.

Your next step: Step 1: check your battery (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Step 2: your wiring · Step 4: what settles you · Step 5: find the words · The whole book on knowing yourself (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-know-yourself)

The fields behind this part

This part draws on 6 of the author’s thirteen fields (the About page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/about) lists them all):

  • Psychology (Tune how you send and receive): How you take words in and send them out, and what helps you feel understood.
  • Neurobiology (Read your state first): Your nervous system’s state comes before your words, and wiring is part of how you are built.
  • Philosophy (Tune how you send and receive): Your honesty, your ask and your tone are up to you. The other person’s answer is up to them.
  • Behavioural science (Read your state first): Try small routines on calm days, like a one-minute reading and a sentence you keep ready.
  • Holistic therapies (Read your state first): Body first, words second. Decide on a calm day what settles you.
  • Economics (See the whole load): Managing yourself costs effort that doesn’t show, and it counts as part of the load.

Two fields, one idea: Philosophy + Neurobiology. If getting revved up or shutting down is a body doing its job, it isn’t a character flaw. That changes what blame means, including the blame you aim at yourself.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

In real life

  • Partners: Sam knows surprise plans make their chest tighten, and says so on a calm day: “A heads-up helps me. It isn’t about you.” Now their partner knows what to try.
  • Family: You need a quiet half hour after a long visit. You say so before you go: “I’ll be good company after a short rest.” It sounds like a plan, not a retreat.
  • Housemates: One housemate needs an hour of quiet after work to recover. The other hears it as being shut out. A one-line note settles it: “Quiet until seven isn’t about you. I’m back after.”
  • Coworkers: Someone thinks best with the agenda a day ahead. They say it once, as how they work and not as an apology: “Could the agenda come the day before?”

Common mix-ups

  • “Knowing myself means finding the right label.” It’s about what helps, not a name. The three layers and a Wave Code are everyday words, not a diagnosis.
  • “‘That’s just how I am’ ends the talk.” It may be true, especially for wiring. It works better as a start: “This is how I’m wired, and here’s what helps.”
  • “If I tell people how I’m wired, they have to manage me.” Telling them helps their words land. You still do your part, and they still have their own needs.
  • “I’m fine” means I’m fine. Sometimes. It can also mean you’ve been tired for so long you stopped noticing. A quick reading each week shows a baseline you’ve got used to.
  • “Looking at myself is selfish.” Every conversation runs through your own state. Knowing it is part of being easier to talk with.
  • “If I need something, I have to justify it.” You don’t. “A heads-up helps me” is enough. A reason is a kindness you can offer, not a fee you owe.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis, a test or treatment, and it can’t tell you whether you’re autistic, have ADHD or anything else, or what anyone else has. If you’d like to understand yourself more deeply, a qualified professional can help, if and when you want that. Nothing here is required, and nothing you try needs to be shared. If talking about any of this with someone ever feels unsafe, or you feel you can’t say no, stop and talk with a trained counselor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counseling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? lists free, private hotlines.

Try this: Pick one reaction you had this week, and write one line for each layer.

“My wiring part is…” “The older part is…” “Today’s part was…”

Then take a one-minute reading of your weather, and write one sentence about what helps you, in your own words. Keep it to yourself for a few days.

When it feels right, share that one sentence with one person, on a calm day.

Know your own wiring → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself) Find your Wavelength → Make your Wiring Card → Today’s Weather, a one-minute self-check → How much are you carrying? → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying) The Calm-Down Kit → Next in the book: Next → (page 58)

What to remember

  • Today has two layers you can work with: your wiring, which stays (work with it), and today’s conditions, which pass (work around them).
  • Check your state before a hard talk. Weather, the three states, the load and the battery are different words for the same thing: how much room you have today.
  • If a feeling is hard to name, start with the body. That is common, and it has a name: alexithymia.
  • Your needs and limits are information. Plan what settles you on a calm day, and say what helps in one short sentence.
  • Different isn’t wrong. A mix-up between two different minds runs both ways, so both of you adjust a little.

Next

Part One · Next

Know yourself: next, shaping who you are becoming

You aren’t finished, and some of who you become is up to you. This part is about choosing a direction, and building small steps that still work on a tired day.

In this chapter

  1. Start with what matters to you
  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words
  3. Name what gets in the way
  4. Make the step tiny, and repeatable
  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then
  6. Ask for support, as information
  7. Look back kindly once a month
  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan
  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back
  10. The ideas, one at a time
  11. You, in all your relationships
  12. Inside you, and between you
  13. In the individual program
  14. The fields behind this part
  15. In real life
  16. Common mix-ups

In short:

  • Start with what matters to you, in two or three plain words, then pick one small goal you can do.
  • Make the step tiny and decide ahead: “If it’s after dinner, then I put my shoes on.”
  • Ask for support as information, and look back kindly once a month.
  • A missed day is information about the plan, not a verdict on you. Change the plan.
  • Set goals inside your circle, and spend your energy where it comes back.

The big ideas: This part mostly teaches “Fix the setup, not the person” and “Notice the quiet incentives”, with help from “Read your state first”. What are the five big ideas? (They are five plain ideas the whole program is built on.)

Wednesday, 9:10pm

You meant to start walking after dinner. You meant to last week, too. Tonight you’re tired, the shoes are by the door, and you tell yourself you’ll begin on Monday.

  1. Start with what matters to you.

    A goal built on someone else’s idea of success is hard to keep up. Before you pick anything, ask: what do I want my days to be like? Write two or three plain words, like calm, close to my family, steady or creative. They are a direction, not a score. Wavelength (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) can help you notice what fills you up and what drains you.

    Dig deeper: values first

  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words.

    Just one. Say it as something you will do, not something you hope will happen: “Walk for ten minutes after dinner,” not “get healthier.” Your own actions are up to you. How other people respond, and how things turn out, are not.

    Dig deeper: one goal, in plain words

  3. Name what gets in the way.

    Use what you learned in Then (page 22) and Now (page 39). Is it your wiring (a plan that ignores how you’re built is built for someone else)? An old rule (“rest has to be earned”)? Or today’s conditions (a tired evening)? Then change the arrangement, never yourself: move the step to the morning, not the person to a better version.

    Dig deeper: what gets in the way

  4. Make the step tiny, and repeatable.

    Small enough to survive your worst week. “Put my shoes on” counts. Tie it to something you already do, and do it often. This is the same idea as the 90-second daily check-in in Chapter I (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1-in-depth) of Part Two: small and often beats big and rare. Start in 10 minutes (spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes) shows how small a whole path can be.

    Dig deeper: tiny, repeatable steps

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: tiny steps count, even the wobbly ones! If you like a game, there’s one where each small kind act moves the ball up the field.

    Tool: Calm football game for small kind acts spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then.

    “If it’s after dinner, then I put my shoes on.” Deciding ahead means one less decision on a tired day, the same idea as the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11), which you make while calm. If a plan isn’t working, that’s information about the plan, not about you. Change the plan.

    Dig deeper: if-then plans

  6. Ask for support, as information.

    Tell one person what you’re trying and what would help: “I’m trying to walk after dinner. Could you ask me about it on Sunday?” It isn’t a demand, they can say no, and you don’t need their agreement to start. Some goals are better with a qualified professional, and asking for one is a sensible step, if and when you want that.

    Dig deeper: asking for support

  7. Look back kindly once a month.

    It mirrors Chapter V (page 172) of Part Two, pointed at yourself. Once a month, take ten minutes: what went well? What kept slipping? Was the gap in the plan, in how much you have right now, or just a one-off week? You don’t add up old misses. You only ask what to try next month.

    Dig deeper: a monthly look at yourself

    Professor Puddles

    Your monthly look is the solo version of the look-back in Chapter V. Borrow its two questions if you like: what kept slipping, and what would have made it easier?

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan.

    A plan that needs you to be harsh with yourself is built on a “second arrow”: the first arrow is the slip itself, and the second is the telling-off you give yourself afterwards, which hurts more and helps less. A missed day is information. Rest is part of the plan, not a prize for finishing. You can shrink a goal, change it or drop it. Nothing here is required, and you can stop any time.

    Dig deeper: kindness as part of the plan

  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back.

    A goal that depends on someone else changing is a wish. Shape each goal around what you can do: “I’ll ask once, kindly, by Friday,” not “They’ll start helping.” Then budget your energy like the limited thing it is. Put more into the people and plans that give back, and less into the ones that only take. That isn’t selfish. It’s how you keep going long enough to reach the goal, and still have something left to give.

    Dig deeper: planning inside your circle

The ideas, one at a time

Each idea above again, with a real-life example, words you could use and one small step. Read one and stop if you like.

zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxmattersqz1. Start with what matters

For example: After their youngest leaves home, a couple each write two words. Hers are “useful, outdoors.” His are “calm, curious.” Suddenly it makes sense that she wants to volunteer and he wants the garden. See Kids grown and gone (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest).

Words you could use: “What I want my days to feel like is ___.”

Try this: Write two plain words for what matters to you right now. Pencil is fine. You can change them.

2. One small goal, in plain words

For example: A student in a shared dorm room wants “to be less messy.” As an action, it becomes “Put my clothes in the basket before bed.” See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).

Words you could use: “My one goal this month is ___.”

Try this: Rewrite one wish as something you will do, starting with “I will…”

3. What gets in the way

For example: A shift worker keeps missing his evening run. It isn’t laziness. His rota (his work timetable) changes every week. He ties the run to “my first day off” instead of “evenings.” See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

Words you could use: “It’s not that I don’t care. The setup doesn’t fit yet.”

Try this: Pick one thing that keeps slipping. Ask: is it my wiring, an old rule, or today’s conditions?

zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxtinyqz4. Tiny and repeatable

For example: Someone on their own after a breakup wants to “get back out there.” The tiny step: one message to one friend every Sunday. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Words you could use: “I’m starting really small, on purpose.”

Try this: Shrink your step until it takes less than two minutes.

5. Decide ahead

For example: A separated parent wants calmer handovers. Her if-then: “If I pull up outside, then I take three slow breaths before I get out of the car.” See Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

Words you could use: “If ___ happens, then I’ll ___.”

Try this: Write one if-then. Pick a cue that happens every day, like the kettle, the front door or brushing your teeth.

zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxsupportqz6. Ask for support

For example: A woman caring for her husband after a stroke asks her brother, “Could you sit with him on Thursday afternoons so I can swim?” Because it is specific, it is easy to say yes or no. See When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

Words you could use: “I’m trying ___. Would you be up for ___? It’s fine to say no.”

Try this: Name one person and one small, specific thing they could do. (If someone uses your goals to check up on you or control you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

7. Look back kindly

For example: A grandmother raising her two grandchildren looks back on the month. Bedtime is working. Homework isn’t. Next month she tries homework at the kitchen table straight after a snack. See Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).

Words you could use: “What went well, what kept slipping, and what will I try next?”

Try this: Put ten minutes in your calendar for the first of next month.

8. Kindness is part of the plan

For example: A sixteen-year-old sets a goal to revise every night, misses three nights and says, “I’m useless.” His grandmother asks, “What would you tell your best friend?” He shrinks the goal to twenty minutes.

Words you could use: “That was a missed day, not a missed life.”

Try this: Next time you miss a step, say one sentence to yourself that you would say to a friend.

9. Inside your circle

For example: You’d like your adult sister to call more. That goal sits outside your circle. Inside it: “I’ll call on the first Sunday of each month, and tell her I’d love her to call too.” See Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts).

Words you could use: “I’d love it if ___. Either way, I’ll ___.”

Try this: Rewrite one goal that depends on someone else, so the next step is yours.

The first of the month

You open your notes. Of the four small things you tried, two stuck and two quietly stopped. Nothing went wrong. You just know now which two need a different setup.

You, in all your relationships

A goal for yourself often touches the people around you. Small steps work everywhere.

  • With yourself: Rest, health, a hobby you dropped, a kinder inner voice.
  • With partners: One small habit you offer, not one you demand. See Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together).
  • With friends: One message a week. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • With family: A regular call, a visit you can keep up, or a first step after years apart. See Reaching out.
  • At work: One comment per meeting, one clear handover note.
  • With money: One small saving habit you control. See Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together).
  • On your own: A week that suits you. See On my own.

Find your own situation in help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship).

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Treat your own routines as a setup you can adjust, not a character test. Notice the defaults and cues that steer you, and let the easy path be the one you want. Pick the step for the energy you really have.
  • Between you and others: Say what you’re trying and what would help, as information. Let people’s answers be theirs, and fix the setup, not the person.

In the individual program

This part goes with the end of the individual program: a gentle first week, then the Individual package, which turns your workpapers into a report written just for you.

Your next step: A gentle first week (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · The Individual package and your report · All six steps · The whole book on knowing yourself (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-know-yourself)

The fields behind this part

This part draws on 6 of the author’s thirteen fields (the About page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/about) lists them all):

  • Behavioural science (Notice the quiet incentives): Habits beat willpower, especially when you’re tired. Cues and defaults steer us more than intentions do.
  • Psychology (Tune how you send and receive): What matters to you, and what you tell yourself when a day goes wrong.
  • Philosophy (Tune how you send and receive): What Is Up to Us, and Aristotle’s idea that we become what we repeatedly do.
  • Business (Fix the setup, not the person): A small, regular review catches problems while they are small.
  • Economics (See the whole load): Attention is limited, so one small goal beats five big ones.
  • Holistic therapies (Read your state first): Small repeated acts are rhythms, and rest is part of the rhythm.

Two fields, one idea: Philosophy + Behavioural science. Aristotle thought we become what we repeatedly do. Character, like a habit, is built by small acts, not by one big decision.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-3-next-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

In real life

  • Partners: One partner wants calmer evenings. They pick one small step, no phones at the table for ten minutes, and say so: “I’m trying this. Would you try it with me?” The other can say yes, not yet or no.
  • Family: You’d like to be in touch with a sibling more. “If it’s Sunday after lunch, then I call for ten minutes” is easier to keep than “I should call more.”
  • Housemates: You want the kitchen to stay clear. Your part is a setup, not willpower: “If I make a drink, then I wash the cup before I sit down.”
  • Coworkers: You’d like to speak up more in meetings. One comment per meeting, written down beforehand from the agenda, is a goal you can actually do.

Common mix-ups

  • “A goal has to be big to count.” Small and repeatable is what survives a bad week. Big goals are often just many small ones.
  • “If I miss a day, I’ve failed.” A missed day tells you about the plan. Ask what got in the way, then adjust the setup.
  • “If I know myself, I should be able to change anything.” Wiring stays. The aim is a goal that fits how you’re built, not a different you.
  • “Asking for support means I couldn’t manage alone.” It’s information that helps others help. People who ask are using the setup well.
  • “A monthly look-back means grading myself.” It’s a look, not a trial. It never adds up old misses.
  • “I’ll start on Monday.” A fresh start can help, but today’s tiny version counts too. Put your shoes on now.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t therapy, coaching or medical advice, and it can’t promise any result. Goals about your health, money, work or a hard stretch in life may deserve a qualified professional, and there’s no shame in asking for one. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared. If a goal ever starts to feel like a weight, you can shrink it or put it down.

Try this: Write two plain words for what matters to you right now.

Write one small goal as something you will do. Then the tiniest first step, and one if-then: “If ___, then I ___.”

Put a ten-minute look-back on the calendar for a month from now. At that look-back, ask: what went well, what kept slipping, and what will I try next?

  • Start with what matters to you, in two or three plain words, then pick one small goal you can do.
  • Make the step tiny and decide ahead: “If it’s after dinner, then I put my shoes on.”
  • Ask for support as information, and look back kindly once a month.
  • A missed day is information about the plan, not a verdict on you. Change the plan.
  • Set goals inside your circle, and spend your energy where it comes back.
