Preface

Preface to Part Two

The work nobody sees: invisible labour at home

Part Two of the book is about the people you share a life, a home or a job with, and it opens here. Running a life takes a lot of work that nobody sees. This preface helps you make that work visible, to yourself and to anyone you share it with, so you can talk about it fairly and kindly.

In this chapter

  1. Unseen work quietly adds up
  2. A lot of it is thinking, not doing
  3. The other person usually just hasn’t seen it
  4. Writing it down isn’t keeping score
  5. Each of you writes only your own side
  6. The borrowed words are there to take the blame away
  7. One small step at a time
  8. It can help in many kinds of shared life
  9. The mental load: what the research says
  10. Inside you, and between you
  11. On your own: your own unseen work
  12. The fields behind this chapter
  13. Where this comes from: the polymath way
  14. In real life
  15. More kinds of shared life
  16. Your situation, in this part of the book
  17. Common mix-ups
  18. Limits and cautions

In short:

  • Running a home takes unseen work: the noticing, remembering and planning that many people call the mental load.
  • The other person usually just hasn’t seen it. This work hides by nature. It isn’t a sign that they don’t care.
  • Each of you writes only your own side of one ordinary week, and you read the two lists together.
  • The list is for seeing, not for billing. Thank each other for the past, and plan next week.

The big ideas: This preface mostly teaches “See the whole load”, with help from “Notice the quiet incentives”. What are the five big ideas?

Sunday, 9pm

Someone notices the laundry is still in the washer, the school forms are due on Tuesday, and the birthday card never got posted. They also notice that nobody else has noticed. The house looks fine. That’s the problem.

Or, living alone: A widower says, “Since my wife died, I notice how many jobs she quietly carried: the birthday cards, the boiler service, knowing who to ring when someone was ill. I never saw them until they stopped getting done.”

  1. Unseen work quietly adds up.

    Remembering appointments, noticing the milk is low, calming a tense moment: none of it shows up on a calendar, so it rarely gets a thank-you. Over months, it piles up. The book calls this pile unbilled debt. Nobody sends a bill for it. You can thank someone for what they carried before; you just don’t bill for the past.

    For example: Marcus remembers every school form, dentist visit and bit of lunch money for their two kids. His husband, Theo, sees two kids who always seem to have what they need. The work is just out of sight.

    Words you could use: “Can I show you some of the things I keep track of? I’m not asking you to pay anything back. I just want you to see them.”

    Try this: Tonight, write down three things you did today that nobody saw. Don’t do anything with the list yet. Just notice.

    Dig deeper: the work that goes unseen

    Professor Puddles

    The easiest way to see unseen work is to write it down for one ordinary week. Each of you logs only your own jobs, and the thinking counts too.

    Workpaper WP-01: Who did what spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-01

  2. A lot of it is thinking, not doing.

    Before a job gets done, someone has to notice it, remember it, plan it and check it happened. That thinking takes real time and energy, even though nobody can see it.

    For example: In a shared flat, Yasmin notices the internet deal is ending, compares plans, picks one and checks it went through. Paying took two minutes. The thinking took an evening.

    Words you could use: “Doing it is the quick part. Remembering it and planning it is the part I’d love some help with.”

    Try this: Pick one job at home and split it into four steps: notice, plan, do, check. Who usually does each step?

    Dig deeper: the kinds of unseen work

  3. The other person usually just hasn’t seen it.

    When this work is done well, nothing seems to happen. So the other person isn’t ignoring it. From where they stand, it looks like things take care of themselves.

    For example: Edna minds her grandchildren three afternoons a week and quietly moves her own doctor visits to fit. Her daughter thinks it all “fits in easily.”

    Words you could use: “I don’t think you’ve been ignoring it. I think it’s been hard to see from where you are.”

    Try this: Ask one person, “What’s something you do that you think I don’t see?” Then just listen, without explaining.

    Dig deeper: why it stays hidden

  4. Writing it down isn’t keeping score.

    The point is for both of you to see the same picture, in the same words, at the same time. Then the talk starts from facts you share, not from two different memories.

    The book calls this shared record a ledger: a plain list of who did what. It’s a way to see, not a bill.

    For example: Two coworkers sharing one job each list a week of tasks. Every client call landed on one person. They don’t argue about last year; they swap Friday calls.

    Words you could use: “I’m not trying to win anything. I’d like us both to be looking at the same list.”

    Try this: Before you show anyone a list, ask yourself: is this to plan next week, or to prove a point? Share it only if the answer is “plan.”

    Dig deeper: why a ledger isn’t a grudge

  5. Each of you writes only your own side.

    Nobody fills in anything for the other person. You each note what you did, then read the two lists together. That keeps it fair and keeps it kind. Each of you also adds the context only you have, like what the week was like, so you both understand rather than judge.

    For example: Arran, Dani and Sol are three partners sharing a home. Each writes only their own list. Reading them together, Sol learns Arran has been calling the landlord every month.

    Words you could use: “I’ve written my side. Would you like to write yours, in your own words, when you’re ready?”

    Try this: Add one line of context to your own list, like “long week at work” or “the kids were ill.” It helps the other person understand, not judge.

    Dig deeper: your side, their side

  6. The borrowed words are there to take the blame away.

    The book uses a few terms from accounting and science because they describe what’s happening without saying whose fault it is. Each one is explained in plain words, and you never need them to use anything here.

    For example: Two brothers share their mum’s care. Instead of “you never help,” one says, “There’s some unseen work here we haven’t looked at.” That’s much easier to hear.

    New together? If words like “ledger” or “debt” feel heavy a few months in, use your own. “Our list” and “the stuff nobody sees” work just as well. The idea stays the same: two people looking at one honest picture, kindly, so nobody has to guess.

    Words you could use: “Let’s look at how it’s set up, not at each other.”

    Try this: Swap one blaming phrase you use, like “you never,” for a plain one, like “this job keeps landing on me.”

    Dig deeper: why the book borrows these words

  7. One small step at a time.

    Each chapter adds one idea and one tool. One week of notes is enough to start. Later come a 90-second daily check-in about how much you were carrying today, a weekly catch-up and a monthly look-back. If you use the monthly look-back later, a few lines a week is all it needs.

    For example: A nurse on nights and a partner on days hardly see each other awake. They start with one week of notes on the fridge. No changes yet.

    Words you could use: “Could we just try one week of notes and see what we notice? We don’t have to change anything yet.”

    Try this: Pick a start day this week and set one reminder on your phone. That’s the whole first step.

    Dig deeper: how the book fits together

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: counting jobs isn’t keeping score. It’s more like a treasure hunt for the work nobody noticed! The quick split check is a good first sniff.

    Tool: Who does what: chore split check spreadloveandacceptance.com/lemonade-stand

  8. It can help in many kinds of shared life.

    Partners, family, roommates, co-parents and coworkers all share unseen work. The examples often use a couple at home, but the ideas fit anyone who shares a load.

    For example: A foster carer tracks family visits, social worker calls and school meetings. A teenager in the home quietly cooks for the younger ones twice a week. Both count.

    Words you could use: “Whatever we are to each other, we share some work. Could we look at it together?”

    Try this: Name one shared load in your life that isn’t a couple: a family group chat, a shared flat, a team at work.

    Dig deeper: who this book is for

Your part, and only your part. You can’t make anyone see the unseen work, and you can’t write their side of the ledger. You can write your own side honestly, say it once, kindly, and then match what you take on to what comes back. If you keep carrying more than your share with nothing in return, stepping back towards your share isn’t a punishment. It protects the energy you need to stay kind. More in Part One: who you are today (page 39)

Friday, after work

“You didn’t have to do all that,” they say, and they mean it kindly. You think: someone did. The list only ever lived in your head, so to them it looked like it took care of itself.

zqaxprefacexxmentalxloadqzThe mental load: what the research says

Many people call the thinking side of home life the mental load: the noticing and planning that come before a job gets done, and the checking after. Knowing the baby needs the next size of clothes. Remembering the form, the jab, the party present. It’s real work, even when it doesn’t look like any.

Studies of couples find some patterns, on average. In couples of a man and a woman, women tend to do more of the noticing and checking (Allison Daminger, 2019). After a first baby, a gap often opens: in one study of working couples, mothers took on most of the new childcare while keeping their paid hours (Jill Yavorsky and colleagues, 2015). Arlie Hochschild called the home work that starts after paid work ends “the second shift.”

There is a fair point on the other side too. Sometimes the parent who knows how things are done holds on to that, without meaning to. Researchers call it gatekeeping. When a parent openly invites the other in, and lets them do it their own way, the other parent tends to do more of the care (Sarah Allen and Alan Hawkins, 1999; Sarah Schoppe-Sullivan and colleagues, 2008).

These are averages across many homes, not a verdict on yours. In your home it may be the other way round, or already even, or shared between two men or two women. That’s why the book asks you to look at your own week on paper, instead of guessing.

For example (made up): Hollie and Gareth have a toddler and a baby, and Gareth works shifts. Their week’s minutes come out nearly even. But Hollie did almost three-quarters of the jobs nobody asked anyone to do. Their week is in Chapter II (page 125).

Words you could use: “You do lots of the doing. It’s the remembering I’d love you to take some of: whole jobs, start to finish.” Or, the other way round: “Show me once how you like it done, then let me do it my way.”

Dig deeper: the mental load, fairly

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Notice everything you carry, including the thinking and feeling work you have never counted. Notice, too, the work others do that you may have missed.
  • Between you and others: Put both lists on one shared, fair page, so nobody has to argue about whose work “counts.” Jobs nobody claims tend to drift to whoever notices first, and a specific thank-you helps keep things steady.

Words you could use: “I want to see what you carry, too, not just what I carry.” “Could we put both our weeks on one page?”

On your own: your own unseen work

You don’t need anyone else to start seeing the unseen. For one week, notice the jobs only you remember: the appointments, the restocking, the smoothing-over. Write them down for yourself, not as a bill.

  • Count it, don’t charge it. The point is to see your real load, so you can plan your energy.
  • Notice which jobs are yours by choice and which just landed on you.
  • Pick one job you could hand back, drop or do less often, and say so kindly.

For example: Nicola, divorced, has the children every other week. On paper, she sees she still buys presents for both sides of the family. She hands his side back, kindly, in one message.

Words you could use: “I’ve noticed I’ve been doing this for both of us. From next month, could you take it on?” Or, to yourself: “That was real work, even if nobody saw it.”

Try this: Circle one job on your list that is yours by choice. Enjoy it. Then circle one that just landed on you, and decide what you’ll do about it. More for people living alone or after a breakup: On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

In the individual program: Step 1: check your battery (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Step 6: kind ways to say no · Part One: your circle of control (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now-in-depth) · The whole book on sharing the load (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-share-the-load)

The fields behind this chapter

Christian, who wrote this book, worked as a government auditor and is a polymath: someone who studied thirteen fields deeply (psychology, philosophy, behavioural science, neurobiology, economics, business, finance, holistic therapies, aromatherapy, the art of debating, politics, music and the healing power of laughter). This chapter grows from 5 of them:

  • Finance (See the whole load): The idea of an unbilled hour: work that was done and logged, but never invoiced, so the client never sees it.
  • Economics (See the whole load): Attention is limited. Every reminder you hold in your head takes up some of it.
  • Psychology (See the whole load): We remember our own effort best.
  • Philosophy (See the whole load): Telling what we know from how things look. In Plato’s Cave, people mistake shadows for the real thing.
  • Business (Notice the quiet incentives): Work that belongs to everyone belongs to no one, and it lands on whoever notices first.

Two fields, one idea: Finance + Psychology. In double-entry bookkeeping, every amount is recorded in two places, and the two must agree. And we each remember our own effort best. Put together: each person keeps their own record, and the two records are read side by side.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/preface-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

Where this comes from: the polymath way

This book is built on a polymath’s habit: looking at very different fields and noticing that the same few roots keep turning up. Those roots are balance, signal and noise, feedback loops, limited capacity, ownership, quiet incentives, and state and setting. A ledger, a nervous system and a conversation look nothing alike, yet each one has a limit, each one can lose a message in the noise, and each one stays steady only when what goes out is matched by what comes back.

Christian saw those roots across thirteen fields. The four newest to the list are the art of debating, politics, music and the healing power of laughter. They shape the gentler parts of the book: how to disagree without a fight, how a small group decides fairly, how tone and tempo change what lands, and how a shared laugh can repair a hard moment.

Read the polymath way · See how every field connects to every other

In real life

  • Partners: One of you keeps track of birthdays, presents and thank-you notes for both families. The other has never had to think about it.
  • Family: One grown-up child handles a parent’s appointments and prescription refills each week. The others see a parent who is “doing fine.”
  • Roommates: One roommate always buys the toilet paper and the dish soap. Nobody asked them to. It just keeps happening.
  • Coworkers: One person books the meetings, takes the notes and follows up afterwards. It isn’t in anyone’s job description.

Words you could use: “I didn’t know you did that. Thank you.” “Can we look at who does the remembering, not just the doing?”

More kinds of shared life

Unseen work turns up wherever people share something:

  • Two mums: one holds the baby’s dates and forms in her head; the other does lots of hands-on care.
  • More than two partners: a job nobody owns lands on whoever notices first. More than two (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two)
  • Friends: one friend always makes the plans and sends the “how are you?” Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends)
  • Teens: walking the dog and minding a sister feels like a lot to them, and like “helping a bit” to adults. For teens (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens)
  • Grandparents and grown-up children: childcare comes with planning work, too. Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children)
  • Adult siblings: one sorts a late parent’s paperwork for months. Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts)
  • Co-parents and carers: packing the right kit for two homes; meetings and reports on top of care. Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Foster and kinship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship)
  • Housemates, coworkers and business partners: one person always notices the bathroom, or chases the invoices. Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room)
  • Illness, different hours, distance, two faiths: the one at home more, or the one who is well, becomes the default; the ill partner manages unseen pain and energy. When one is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours) · Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance) · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths)

Words you could use: “I don’t need it to be even. I need it to be seen.”

Find your own starting point: Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) · How it fits your relationships (spreadloveandacceptance.com/relationships).

Your situation, in this part of the book

Some situations get their own section in Part Two:

  • Faith, culture, elders and in-laws: Chapter I (page 103)
  • Small children or a new baby: Chapter II (page 125)
  • Two homes after a split, and step-parents: Chapter III (page 147)
  • Money between you: Chapter IV (page 168)
  • A couple and a housemate: Chapter IV (page 168)
  • New together, or about to move in: Chapter V (page 186)
  • Grandparents raising a grandchild: Chapter V (page 187)

Common mix-ups

  • “If it mattered, they would have asked for help.” Unseen work is often hidden from the person doing it, too, until it’s written down.
  • “Writing it down means I’m angry.” It means you want you both to see the same picture.
  • “It has to be exactly 50/50.” The goal is a split you can both see and both agree to, not a perfect half.
  • “Mental work doesn’t count, only chores do.” Remembering, planning and checking take real time and energy. Put them on the list.
  • “We should start by going over the last ten years.” Start with one ordinary week. You can thank someone for the past without trying to settle it.
  • “The one doing less doesn’t care.” Usually they just can’t see it yet. Nobody here is the villain. Once you’ve both seen it, what you do next is a choice you make together.

Words you could use: “I don’t think either of us is the bad guy here. We just haven’t seen the same picture yet.”

Try this: Each of you, on your own, list the things you did this week that nobody saw. Then swap lists.

Next, read the other list slowly and say one thing on it you hadn’t noticed before.

Then pick one item from their list and say thank you for it, in a specific way.

If writing things down isn’t your style, a ten-minute talk over a cup of coffee with the same questions works too.

Keep it light. This is a first look, not a verdict. The fixing comes later in the book.

Turn it into a gentle week-long log: Who did what → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01) How to say a specific thank-you → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward)

Limits and cautions

These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about the split ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A list should never be demanded, checked over your shoulder, or used to keep track of where you go or what you spend. If that is happening, it isn’t a ledger. It’s control, and it’s not your fault. Signs to look out for. If you are a counsellor or group leader using this book with others, see For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors).

What to remember

  • Running a home takes unseen work: the noticing, remembering and planning that many people call the mental load.
  • The other person usually just hasn’t seen it. This work hides by nature. It isn’t a sign that they don’t care.
  • Each of you writes only your own side of one ordinary week, and you read the two lists together.
  • The list is for seeing, not for billing. Thank each other for the past, and plan next week.

I

Part Two · Chapter I

Why we get out of tune: communication at home

Why two kind, reasonable people can end up in a tangle neither of them started, and how to get back in step.

In this chapter

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words
  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part
  3. Three things knock you out of tune
  4. Stress changes your station
  5. Nobody has to be wrong
  6. Get back in tune before you carry on
  7. Go back in with a clear sentence
  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune
  9. Faith, culture and family voices
  10. Inside you, and between you
  11. On your own: your side of the tuning
  12. The fields behind this chapter
  13. In real life
  14. More kinds of shared life
  15. Common mix-ups

In short:

  • A clash often isn’t about the words. Pace, tone and urgency can be out of step even when both of you mean well.
  • Nobody has to be wrong. Name it (“we’re out of tune”), pause with a time to come back, and slow down.
  • Go back in with one clear sentence: a fact, a feeling and an ask.
  • A 90-second daily check-in keeps small drifts small.

The big ideas: This chapter mostly teaches “Tune how you send and receive”, with help from “Read your state first”. What are the five big ideas?

Tuesday, 6:40pm

“I said I’d do it.” “I know, I’m just asking when.” Four sentences later, nobody is talking about the bins any more, and neither of you can point to the moment it turned.

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words.

    Two people can each say something reasonable and still clash, because the tone underneath doesn’t match. It’s like two radios slightly out of tune: together they make a crackle that neither one was making alone.

    For example: Two housemates. “Is anyone using the oven tonight?” “Why, did I leave a mess?” A plain question was heard as a complaint.

    Words you could use: “I think the words were fine. Something in how we said them got crossed.”

    Try this: After your next small clash, ask yourself: was it the words, or the way they came out?

    Dig deeper: the radio static

  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part.

    Radios on very different stations don’t whistle at each other. The whistle comes when they are close but not quite matched. People who know each other well can still clash. Research suggests we check our meaning less with people we’re close to, because we assume they already understand us.

    For example: Two sisters who talk every day clash over holiday plans far more than they ever do with cousins they see once a year. Being close means more overlap.

    Words you could use: “I think I assumed you knew what I meant. Let me say it more clearly.”

    Try this: With someone close, check one meaning today: “Just so I’ve got it right, you mean…?”

    Dig deeper: why close can be noisy

    Tidbit

    Ooh, Tidbit loves this one: compare your daily rhythms and see whose engine runs fast in the morning and whose at night. Different speeds aren’t wrong, just different!

    Tool: Compare your daily rhythms spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/frequency-calibration

  3. Three things knock you out of tune.

    How fast you’re talking. The tone, when a simple update is heard as a complaint. And how urgent it feels: “when you get a chance” can mean tonight to one person and next week to the other.

    For example: A business partner texts “Need to talk” between two meetings. The other partner reads it as a crisis and can’t sleep. It was about a printer. A text loses most of the tone, so urgency is easy to misread.

    Words you could use: “By when would be good?” “Is this an update, or a worry?”

    Try this: Add a time to your next request. Not “at some point,” but “by Friday.”

    Dig deeper: pace, tone and urgency

  4. Stress changes your station.

    When you’re tense, you may talk faster and be more likely to hear a pause as a snub. When you’re tired and flat, your replies get slower and shorter. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, helps you guess which one you’re in. It’s a best guess, not a reading.

    For example: A dad gets home from a night shift and answers his teenager with one word. The teen hears “he doesn’t care.” He is just running on empty.

    Words you could use: “I’m running low right now. It’s not about you. Can we talk after I’ve slept?”

    Try this: Before a tricky talk, name your state to yourself: calm, revved up or running on empty.

    Dig deeper: how stress shifts your tune

  5. Nobody has to be wrong.

    Two radios that both work fine will still crackle if they’re slightly off. Arguing about whose fault the static is won’t clear it. Retuning (getting back in step) will.

    For example: A grandmother tells her grown-up son, “You look tired.” She means care. He hears “you can’t cope.” Neither of them is wrong about what they meant or heard.

    Words you could use: “I don’t think either of us meant it that way. Can we try that again?”

    Try this: In your next clash, say “we” instead of “you”: “We got crossed there.”

    Dig deeper: taking the blame out

  6. Get back in tune before you carry on.

    Say it out loud: “I think we’re out of sync.” Check how tense you feel. Either of you can call a pause, and the person who paused names a time to come back. Gently slow down, with shorter turns and more pauses. Only then go back to the actual topic.

    For example: Two dorm roommates agree on a pause word, “static,” on a calm day. Mid-argument about noise, one says it. They stop, and come back at 9pm as agreed.

    Words you could use: “I need ten minutes. I’ll come back at half past.”

    Try this: Agree a pause word with someone today, while you are both calm.

    Dig deeper: the four steps to retune

  7. Go back in with a clear sentence.

    When you return to the topic, say the fact, how you feel, and what you’d like. “The bins go out early on Wednesday morning. I get anxious when they’re late. Could you put them out tonight?”

    For example: A co-parent texts: “The swim kit wasn’t in the bag. I felt stressed at drop-off. Could you pack it on Sunday nights?” A fact, a feeling, an ask.

    Words you could use: “The fact is… I feel… Could we…?”

    Try this: Write one fact, feeling and ask sentence about something small, before you need it.

    Dig deeper: going back in

    Professor Puddles

    When you go back in, one clear sentence beats a speech. This workpaper helps you shape it before you say it.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune.

    A short chat each day, like the 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), can make tiny corrections before small things drift into a big argument. Habit research suggests small routines at a regular time are easier to keep than big ones done rarely. The quiet, easy stretches are the ones that drift most, so keep it going even when nothing seems wrong (see Complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency)).

    For example: A long-distance couple in two time zones send one 90-second voice note each morning. It’s tiny, but it keeps them in step.

    Words you could use: “Today I was carrying quite a lot. One thing I liked today was…”

    Try this: Pick a time and a cue, like right after dinner, and try the check-in for three days.

    Dig deeper: staying in tune

Your part, and only your part. You control what you send, whether you check how it landed, and whether you step out to retune. You don’t control how it’s heard or how fast the other person settles. Matching energy here means matching care and effort, never volume: if someone gets louder, you don’t have to follow. Stay at your level, and give the conversation the energy it gives back. More in Part One: who you are today (page 39)

Saturday, 10am

“We should clear out the spare room at some point.” One of you meant this month. The other heard today and has already cancelled their plans in their head. By lunchtime you’re both upset about a room nobody has touched.

zqaxchapterx1xxfaithxcultureqzFaith, culture and family voices

For many couples, faith is where they turn first. If you share a faith, it can be one of your strongest tools for staying in tune.

  • A shared rhythm: praying together, or a quiet moment after worship, can be your daily check-in.
  • A pause with a purpose: some couples pray, each on their own, before they come back to a hard talk. The pause still has a time to come back.
  • Your community: a pastor, imam, rabbi, priest or trusted elder can be a good first person to talk to. Many can also suggest a trained counsellor who shares your faith.

For example (made up): Emeka and Ngozi, married 26 years, do their monthly look-back on a Sunday after church, over lunch. When a talk gets heated, either of them can say, “Let’s pray on it and come back at eight.” And they do.

Culture shapes how you talk, too. In many families, respect for elders decides who can speak plainly to whom. One habit helps: each of you speaks to your own parents and relatives, after you’ve agreed the message together.

Words you could use: “Can we pray about this and talk again tonight?” “Mum, we love you, and we’ve thought about it carefully. This year we’ll visit in August, not at Easter.”

From two faiths or cultures? See Two faiths or cultures, one family (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths). Dig deeper: faith, elders and family far away

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Know your own pace, your usual tone and what “soon” means to you. Notice when stress speeds you up or slows you down.
  • Between you and others: When a clash starts, treat it as a tuning problem, not a moral failing. Retune together, then translate what you meant into words the other person can hear.

Words you could use: “I think this is a tuning problem, not a you problem.” “What did you hear me say? I want to check it came out right.”

On your own: your side of the tuning

Getting out of tune takes two, but retuning can start with one. You can learn your own pace, tone and urgency, so you notice when you’re the one running fast or slow.

  • Learn your early signs of drifting: a tight chest, a clipped reply, wanting to win.
  • Learn how you take words in best, and say it once: “I hear things better in writing.”
  • When you drift, step out, settle and come back. You don’t need anyone’s permission to retune yourself.

For example: Hamid lives alone and notices his texts to friends come out short when he’s tired. Now he waits until morning to answer anything that matters.

Words you could use: “I’m tired, so I might sound shorter than I mean. Can I reply properly tomorrow?”

Try this: For one day, notice the first sign in your body that you’re drifting. Write it down. More for people on their own: On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

In the individual program: Step 2: get to know your wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Step 4: plan what settles you · Part One: who you are today (page 39) · The whole book on talking it through (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-talk-it-through)

The fields behind this chapter

This chapter draws on 5 of the author’s thirteen fields (see the Preface (page 74) or the About page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/about)):

  • Psychology (Tune how you send and receive): The gap between intent and impact: why a clear, kind sentence can still land as an attack, once pace, tone or urgency slips.
  • Neurobiology (Read your state first): How stress changes your frequency, and how you sound and hear.
  • Philosophy (Fix the setup, not the person): Nobody has to be wrong. Zhuangzi’s Empty Boat: much of the time, the bump was no one’s plan.
  • Behavioural science (Tune how you send and receive): Small and often. A small routine at a regular time is easier to keep.
  • Holistic therapies (Read your state first): Body first, argument second. Settle your own state before you go back to the talk.

Two fields, one idea: Neurobiology + Psychology. A tired body changes how words sound and how they’re heard. So the same sentence can be fine on Saturday and a fight on Tuesday. Check your state, then say it.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

In real life

  • Partners: “Did you pay the gas bill?” is meant as a reminder. After a long day, it lands as “you forgot again.”
  • Family: A parent asks, “Are you coming on Sunday?” They mean it as a simple question. Their grown-up child hears guilt.
  • Roommates: A message says, “Can we talk about the kitchen?” One roommate meant a quick chat. The other spends all afternoon worrying.
  • Coworkers: “Quick question” arrives at 5:55pm. The sender meant tomorrow is fine. The reader thinks it’s urgent and stays late.

Words you could use: “I meant that as a question, not a complaint. Sorry it came out sharp.”

More kinds of shared life

Getting out of tune happens wherever people talk often:

  • Two dads: “Did you call the school?” is a reminder to one and a test to the other.
  • Three partners: two speak fast and one slowly, so the slow one gets talked over. More than two (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two)
  • Friends: a one-word reply after a long message reads as cold, when they were just busy. Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends)
  • Gaming and phones: “Five more minutes” means five to one person and a match to the other. Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together)
  • Teens and parents: a parent’s worry comes out fast and sounds like anger. For teens (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens)
  • Adult siblings: after years apart, an old nickname lands like an old fight. Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts)
  • Foster and kinship carers: a child who has been hurt may hear a raised voice as danger, even when it isn’t. Foster and kinship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship)
  • Different hours, illness, two faiths: a tired shift worker, a partner in pain, or two family styles of speaking can all shift the tune. Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours) · When one is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Two faiths

Find your own starting point: Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship).

Common mix-ups

  • “Retuning means giving in.” It doesn’t. You still come back to the topic. You just come back when you can hear each other.
  • “If we’re out of sync, one of us must be wrong.” Two fair points in two different tones can still clash.
  • “Slowing down means I don’t care.” Slowing down is how you show you want to get it right.
  • “A pause means the topic is dropped.” A pause always comes with a time to come back.
  • “We should push through while we’re on the subject.” Pushing on through static usually makes more static.

Try this: Next time a conversation starts to go wrong, pause and say so kindly, instead of pushing through.

Before then, agree on a shared phrase, like “I think we’re out of tune.” That way it feels like a signal, not a criticism.

For one week, each of you notes one moment you felt out of step. At the end, compare: was it mostly pace, tone or urgency?

When someone says “when you get a chance,” kindly ask, “By when would be good?”

The step-by-step reset (the Carrier Wave Decoder) → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) Say it so it lands → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) The 90-second daily check-in →

Words you could use: “I think we’re out of tune. Can we slow down?” “I want to get this right, so I’m going to go slower.”

A limit to keep in mind: These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking things through ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A pause is for both of you. If one person is never allowed to pause, or a “pause” is used to punish with days of silence, that isn’t retuning. Signs to look out for.

What to remember

  • A clash often isn’t about the words. Pace, tone and urgency can be out of step even when both of you mean well.
  • Nobody has to be wrong. Name it (“we’re out of tune”), pause with a time to come back, and slow down.
  • Go back in with one clear sentence: a fact, a feeling and an ask.
  • A 90-second daily check-in keeps small drifts small.

II

Part Two · Chapter II

Is the split working? A fair look at chores at home

One gentle question: can the way you share the work keep going, or is one of you quietly running on empty?

In this chapter

  1. Look at the month, not last night
  2. Three things go in
  3. Balance: how the hours split
  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?
  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is
  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1
  7. Start with the biggest shortfall
  8. It judges the setup, never a person
  9. Words this chapter uses
  10. Inside you, and between you
  11. On your own: is your own load working?
  12. The fields behind this chapter
  13. In real life
  14. Common mix-ups
  15. Small children and a new baby
  16. If only one of you wants to try this
  17. More for your situation

In short:

  • Look at the month, not last night. Use what you both wrote down, not memory.
  • Three things go in: balance (how the hours split), ownership (does each job have a name?) and stress (how full each tank is).
  • One number comes out, from 0 to 1. Start with whichever part pulled it down most.
  • It judges the setup, never a person. It’s where a talk starts, not how one ends.

The big ideas: This chapter mostly teaches “See the whole load” and “Fix the setup, not the person”, with help from “Read your state first”. What are the five big ideas?

Any given week

One of you is quietly doing eleven small things a day that the other has never had to think about. When the other one says it feels even, they mean it. From inside each person’s own week, it does.

  1. Look at the month, not last night.

    When people ask “Is this working?”, the answer usually comes from whatever happened most recently. This chapter asks a calmer question, using what you both wrote down. Re-ask it every few months, even when things seem fine, because a split that worked once can quietly go stale.

    For example: Two housemates had one awful week of dishes. The whole month showed three fine weeks and one exam week.

    Words you could use: “Can we look at the whole month before we decide anything?”

    Try this: Put a short check in your calendar for about a month from now.

    Dig deeper: what the check is for

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: one bad evening isn’t the whole story. Give it a month, then run the check together, slowly, with a snack.

    Workpaper CALC-01: Is the setup working for everyone? spreadloveandacceptance.com/is-the-setup-working

  2. Three things go in.

    How evenly the hours are shared. Whether every regular job has a clear owner (the job list, One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job)). And how stressed each of you already is from everything else going on.

    A workpaper is one of the site’s free fill-in worksheets. You don’t need any of them to start. Rough notes on paper work too.

    Words you could use: “Let’s each bring our own numbers, so neither of us has to guess.”

    Try this: Open the three worksheets once, just to see what they ask.

    Dig deeper: where each number comes from

  3. Balance: how the hours split.

    From your week-long logs, work out each person’s share of the hours. An even split scores 1. One person doing everything scores 0. It doesn’t matter which person is doing more. If you agreed an uneven split that suits you (say, one of you works longer hours outside the home), compare against that split instead.

    For example: Three partners log 30 hours of home jobs: 15, 9 and 6. An even share is 10 each.

    Words you could use: “I’m not keeping score of you. I just want us both to see the hours.”

    Try this: Log one week each, and include the small jobs that take under ten minutes.

    Three or more of you? Compare each person’s share with an even share (100 ÷ number of people), or with a split you agreed. The Lemonade Stand (spreadloveandacceptance.com/lemonade-stand), a free page where each person lists their hours, does the arithmetic.

    Dig deeper: the balance score

  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?

    Each job gets two names: the owner, who does the job start to finish, and a backstop, who notices if it slipped and gently checks in (never a supervisor). It can be the same person, though a second name gives the job a gentle check. Count the jobs that have an owner, then divide by all the jobs on the list. (The backstop is a good habit on top, but the count only needs the owner.) Leave jobs nobody owns on the list. They are the ones that matter most.

    A decision you make together, like which school, can be marked “Both (decide together)”. It counts as owned, because a decision needs both voices. A job that needs doing gets one name.

    For example: Two sisters care for their dad. Nobody owned his prescription, so each thought the other had ordered it.

    Words you could use: “Can we put a name next to this one, so it doesn’t fall between us?”

    Try this: Find one job with no name, and give it an owner and a backstop today.

    Dig deeper: the ownership score

    Professor Puddles

    A job without a name tends to land on whoever notices first. Write one owner next to each job, and the guessing stops.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is.

    Each of you rates how full your own stress tank is with How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying). A higher score means more stress. Under 0.30 is low, 0.30 up to 0.60 is moderate, and 0.60 or more is high. The score uses the average of your scores. But if either of you is at 0.60 or more, talk about that first, even when the score looks fine. A setup that only works when you’re both well rested isn’t one that can last, so more stress lowers the result.

    For example: A grandmother raising two grandchildren scores 0.70. Her son, who helps at weekends, scores 0.35. Her 0.70 is the headline.

    Words you could use: “My tank is high this week. Can we plan around that, not around the average?”

    Try this: Each of you scores your own tank on the same day, before looking at the other’s.

    Dig deeper: the stress score

  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1.

    0.70 or above: working well, the setup is holding. From 0.40 up to 0.70: needs a look, something is drifting, often who owns what. Below 0.40: needs a rethink, together. (The result is called the setup score. It looks like a probability, but it isn’t one. It’s a simple weighted sum.)

    A weighted sum means each part counts for a set share: the hours count most, then the owners, then stress.

    For example: Two friends who run a café score 0.55. Nothing is broken, but something is drifting.

    Words you could use: “This number is about our setup, not about us.”

    Try this: Write the date next to your number, so you can compare next month.

    Dig deeper: the formula and what each range means

  7. Start with the biggest shortfall.

    The single number matters less than which of the three parts pulled it down most. In the middle band that is often ownership, which is why the calculator suggests One owner per job first. Once you’ve both seen it, what you do next is a choice you make together.

    The shortfall is how far one part fell below the most it could add.

    For example: Separated parents score 0.62. Their biggest gap: nobody owns school forms. They fix only that.

    Words you could use: “Which part pulled the number down most? Let’s start there.”

    Try this: Choose one small change, not five.

    Dig deeper: reading your result

  8. It judges the setup, never a person.

    The number isn’t a verdict on who’s better or whether the relationship works. It’s where a conversation starts, never how one ends. These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about the split ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

    For example: One partner sees 0.35: “So I’m the problem.” The other: “No. The bathroom has no owner, and you work nights.”

    Words you could use: “Whatever this shows, I’m on your side.”

    Try this: Before you start, agree that either of you can say “pause” and come back later.

    Dig deeper: what the number is not

Your part, and only your part. The score describes the setup you share, but your levers are your own: your jobs, your hours and what you agree to take on. You can propose a fix; you can’t make the other person accept it. If the balance stays one-sided, step your load back towards your share on purpose, and say so kindly. Matching effort with effort protects your stress tank, and your tank is part of the score too. More in Part One: who you are today (page 39)

Sunday evening

Two week-long logs and two cups of tea. One list has 31 rows. The other has 18. Nobody says anything for a moment. Then one of you says, “I honestly didn’t know about half of these.”

Words this chapter uses

  • Log: a simple list of the jobs you did this week and roughly how long each took.
  • Owner: the person who does a job from start to finish, including remembering it.
  • Backstop: the person who notices if a job slipped and gently checks in. A helper, never a boss.
  • Stress tank: how much stress you are already carrying from the rest of life.
  • Setup: the way you share the work right now. It can always be changed.
  • Setup score: one number from 0 to 1 that sums up the three readings. It describes the setup, never a person.

Invisible jobs count too. Planning meals, remembering birthdays, booking the vet and noticing the soap is running low are all work, even though nobody sees them happen. Put them in your log.

Words you could use: “I’d like to add the thinking jobs to our list, like remembering and planning. They take time too.”

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: See your own share honestly, from what you wrote down rather than from memory. See the way you share work as a setup you can redesign, not a flaw in you.
  • Between you and others: Put both people’s numbers on one page, and read the result as a note about the setup, never a verdict on a person. Clear owners leave less room for blame.

On your own: is your own load working?

This chapter asks whether a shared setup can last. You can ask the same about your own week: are you spending more energy than comes back in?

  • Add up what you carry: jobs, people and worries.
  • Set it beside what refills you: rest, help, and people who give back.
  • If it runs in the red, change your side: drop, delay, ask or say no kindly. A limit is a statement about supply, not about your worth.

For example: After a breakup, Leanne has her kids every other week, and fills the quiet weeks with favours for friends. Writing it down showed her she never rests. More in On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Words you could use: “I’d love to help, and I can’t this week. Can I let you know next week?”

Try this: Tonight, write three things that drained you this week and one thing that refilled you.

In the individual program: Step 1: check your battery (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Step 6: kind ways to say no · Part One: matching energy (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now-in-depth) · The whole book on sharing the load (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-share-the-load)

The fields behind this chapter

This chapter draws on 6 of the author’s thirteen fields (see the Preface or the About page). The first few:

  • Finance (See the whole load): Like a small shop asking whether it can keep paying its bills, month after month. The chapter reads the setup that way, never as a verdict on the people.
  • Business (Fix the setup, not the person): Ownership clarity: one owner per job, borrowed from project work, and the maker-and-checker habit from internal controls. Every regular job gets a person who does it and a backstop who notices if it slipped.
  • Neurobiology (Read your state first): Leftover stress: a quick self-rating of the stress you’re already carrying. It borrows the idea that stress builds up in the body, but it doesn’t measure your body.
  • Economics (See the whole load): Limited capacity and the safety margin.

Two fields, one idea: Business + Economics. Unowned work falls to whoever notices first, every time. That’s what turns a fixable imbalance into a repeating one, so the check counts owners, not just the hours.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

In real life

  • Partners: After a new baby arrives, the hours tip heavily one way without anyone deciding it. The check can show it before resentment builds.
  • Family: Two siblings share care for a parent. One lives nearby and does most of the visits. Writing down the hours helps them rebalance in other ways, like paperwork and phone calls.
  • Roommates: Everyone agrees cleaning matters, but nobody owns the bathroom. The ownership score shows the gap straight away.
  • Coworkers: Two people share one role. The same three questions still work: how the hours split, who owns what, and how stretched each person is.
  • Two dads: With no old script for who does what, nothing was decided. One of them quietly took on all the school messages.
  • More than two partners: In a home of three or more, “someone will do it” often means nobody does. Owners matter even more. See More than two (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).
  • Foster and kinship carers: Meetings, forms and contact visits are real work. See Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).
  • Shift workers: Hours can look even while sleep is not. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).
  • When one of you is ill: Share by energy, and agree an uneven split on purpose. See When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).
  • Dorm roommates: A room agreement with names next to jobs settles most of it. See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).

Words you could use: “I think the way we split things worked before, and life changed. Can we look at it again together?”

Common mix-ups

  • “A low number means the relationship is failing.” It only means the current setup needs changing. Setups change all the time.
  • “A high number means nobody can complain.” A good score never silences anyone. If something feels wrong, say so.
  • “We can just guess the numbers.” A guessed number is really just a feeling with a decimal point. Use your written logs.
  • “Taking unowned jobs off the list will help.” It raises the number and changes nothing at home.
  • “One of us can fill it in for both.” Each person writes their own log and scores their own stress tank.
  • “Fair means exactly 50/50.” Fair is what you both agree to, with eyes open. An uneven split you chose together can be fair. Chapter IV covers the kinds of fair.
  • “The backstop checks up on the owner.” No. The backstop only notices if something slipped, and asks kindly. It is help, not a check on someone.

zqaxchapterx2xxsmallxchildrenqzSmall children and a new baby

Small children bring a flood of new jobs, and most of them are thinking jobs: the nursery bag, the jabs, the party invites, the next size of clothes, the night wakings. That’s why the mental load (see the Preface (page 84)) often grows after a baby arrives, usually without anyone deciding it.

  • Log the kid jobs too, with the thinking time. Nights count.
  • Hand over whole jobs, not tasks: the clothes and sizes, the nursery bag, the GP and jabs. The new owner does the noticing too, in their own way.
  • Baby on the way? Write your first job list together before the birth, plan the nights, and agree to look again at six weeks, three months, and before either of you goes back to work.
  • In the first weeks, share by energy, not hours. Whoever was up in the night gets the rest; the other takes the morning.

For example (made up): Hollie and Gareth have Alfie, 3, and Poppy, 8 months. Gareth is a paramedic on shifts. Their logged minutes come out nearly even, but Hollie did almost three-quarters of the jobs nobody asked for. They don’t move minutes. They move one whole job, the children’s clothes, to Gareth.

Words you could use: “Could you own the nursery bag from now on, including noticing when we’re low on nappies? I won’t check it.”

Dig deeper: small children, new babies and shift work

zqaxchapterx2xxonexpersonqzIf only one of you wants to try this

That is common, and you can still start. Log your own week and score your own tank. Then share one small thing you noticed, without asking the other person to agree with your numbers.

For example: A dad noticed he spent five hours a week driving his teenage son around. He just said so, and they agreed a bus pass for two days a week. See Teens (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens).

Words you could use: “I tried writing down my week, just for me. Can I show you one thing I noticed?”

Try this: Share one finding, not the whole list. Then let it rest for a few days.

If the other person refuses to talk about the split at all, ever, or makes you feel afraid for raising it, that isn’t a setup problem. Please read Not safe at home?

More for your situation

Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together) · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Grandparents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grandparents) · Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · Empty nest (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest) · At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

Try this: Each of you logs one week in Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01), first. The number only means something if you each wrote your own.

Next, fill in the job list in One owner per job together, including any jobs nobody owns yet.

Then each of you scores how full your own stress tank is in How much are you carrying? on the same day.

Put the three numbers into the calculator. Look first at the biggest shortfall, pick one small change together, and check again in a month.

What to remember

  • Look at the month, not last night. Use what you both wrote down, not memory.
  • Three things go in: balance (how the hours split), ownership (does each job have a name?) and stress (how full each tank is).
  • One number comes out, from 0 to 1. Start with whichever part pulled it down most.
  • It judges the setup, never a person. It’s where a talk starts, not how one ends.

III

Part Two · Chapter III

Full tanks and different angles: stress and perspective

Why some reactions are bigger than what caused them, and why two people can see the same moment so differently.

In this chapter

  1. A full tank overflows
  2. Some stress is left over from earlier
  3. Check your stress tank in a minute
  4. Three everyday states
  5. There are seven angles on the same moment
  6. Both views can be true
  7. Say it instead of making each other guess
  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”
  9. Words this chapter uses
  10. Inside you, and between you
  11. On your own: reading your own tank
  12. The fields behind this chapter
  13. In real life
  14. Common mix-ups
  15. Two homes: co-parenting after a split
  16. If only one of you wants to try this
  17. More for your situation

In short:

  • A full tank overflows. Stress left over from earlier makes small things feel big.
  • Check your tank in a minute, and say the band out loud instead of making others guess.
  • Two people can see one moment from different angles, and both views can be true.
  • A full tank means “later,” not “never”: pause, name a time, and come back.

The big ideas: This chapter mostly teaches “Read your state first”, with help from “Tune how you send and receive”. What are the five big ideas?

Thursday, 5:15pm

They ask, perfectly pleasantly, whether you remembered to call the dentist. Your reaction is much bigger than the question deserved, and you can hear it happening while it happens.

  1. A full tank overflows.

    If you’re already tired, stretched or stressed from somewhere else, a small question can get a big reaction. That’s human. Anything decided in that moment is worth coming back to once you’ve both calmed down.

    For example: A nurse gets home after a night shift. Her housemate asks, “Did you see my message?” She snaps. It wasn’t the message. It was twelve hours on her feet.

    Words you could use: “Sorry. That was bigger than the question. I’m running on empty.”

    Try this: Notice one moment this week when your reaction was bigger than its cause.

    Dig deeper: how full your tank is

  2. Some stress is left over from earlier.

    Ask yourself: how much of this feeling is about the thing in front of me, and how much did I bring in with me? “I’m upset about the dishes” and “I’m exhausted, and the dishes are what I noticed” are different problems.

    Some of what we bring in is much older: an understanding from growing up, like “whoever notices the mess has to clean it.” If a feeling seems a lot older than the moment, Where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) helps you find where it started.

    For example: A teenager has a hard day at school, comes home, and explodes because a brother took the phone charger. The charger is the last drop, not the whole tank.

    Words you could use: “I think I brought this in with me. Give me ten minutes.”

    Try this: Before you react, ask: “How much of this is from earlier?”

    Dig deeper: leftover stress

    Professor Puddles

    Before a hard talk, check how full your own tank is. Five quick questions, about two minutes, and you’ll know whether now is the time.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Check your stress tank in a minute.

    How much are you carrying? measures how full your stress tank is. A higher score means more stress in the tank. Score five things from 0 to 4: sleep, work elsewhere, any unsettled argument, how your body feels, and time pressure today. Add them up and divide by 20. Under 0.30 is low. From 0.30 up to 0.60 is moderate. 0.60 or more is high. If it has been high for a long time, it can start to feel normal, so a quick reading each week is worth it.

    For example: A man caring for his wife after surgery scores 0.65 three days in a row. That tells him he needs help, not more effort.

    Words you could use: “I checked my tank. I’m in the high band today.”

    Try this: Score yourself tomorrow morning, before you look at your phone.

    Dig deeper: the stress-tank score

  4. Three everyday states.

    Calm and connected. Revved up. Running on empty. Knowing which one you’re in tells you whether now is a good time to talk. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, helps you make a best guess. These labels come from polyvagal theory, whose main claims are still debated by scientists. Here they are only everyday words, not a medical model.

    For example: In a long-distance couple, one partner takes the video call at midnight his time. He is often running on empty. They move the hard talks to weekend mornings.

    Words you could use: “I’m revved up right now. Can we talk after a walk?”

    Try this: Find one body clue for each state, like a tight jaw for “revved up.”

    Dig deeper: the three states

  5. There are seven angles on the same moment.

    Tiredness, time pressure, history, what home was like growing up, your sense of fairness, how you communicate, and stress from outside. Many arguments are two people looking from different angles, each sure the other sees what they see. The See it from their side (spreadloveandacceptance.com/perspective-shifter) page (the Perspective Shifter), built on these seven angles, helps you picture how the same moment might look from the other side, with questions to ask instead of guesses.

    For example: Planning the holidays, one parent sees it from family habit (“We always go to my mum’s”). The other sees it from fairness (“We went to yours last year”).

    Words you could use: “Which angle are you seeing this from?”

    Try this: Guess which of the seven angles you look from most often.

    Dig deeper: the seven angles

  6. Both views can be true.

    You can each be right about what you see and still be looking at different parts of the same thing. The question isn’t “Who’s right?” but “Which angle are you seeing this from?”

    For example: Two adult brothers argue about their late mother’s house. One sees memories. The other sees bills. Both are real.

    Words you could use: “You’re right about what you see. Can I tell you what I see?”

    Try this: Say the other person’s view back to them before you give yours.

    Dig deeper: two true views

  7. Say it instead of making each other guess.

    Before a hard conversation, each of you says how full your stress tank is and which angle you’re seeing things from. It works best before you start, not in the middle.

    For example: Two coworkers start a tense meeting with one sentence each about their tank and angle. The meeting is shorter, and calmer.

    Words you could use: “Before we start: I’m about half full today, and I’m seeing this from the time angle.”

    Try this: Use that one-line opener once this week.

    Dig deeper: using both together

    Tidbit

    Tidbit’s tip: say your number out loud, like “I’m a seven today.” It’s quick, and nobody has to guess!

    Tool: How am I right now? A mood and energy check spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”

    A high score is a reason to pause, never a way out of the talk. Say when you’ll come back, and the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) can help in the meantime. After your calming steps, check your tank again. Under 0.50, go back at the time you said. From 0.50 to 0.59, if you still feel hot, take another round. Still 0.60 or more after two rounds? That’s okay. Pick a new time, and say when.

    For example: A dad and his 14-year-old get heated about phone time. He says, “I’m too wound up. Let’s talk at seven.” At seven, he knocks on her door.

    Words you could use: “I need a break. I’ll come back at seven. I promise.”

    Try this: Whenever you pause, name the time you’ll come back.

    Dig deeper: pausing without avoiding

Your part, and only your part. Your stress tank is the only one you can empty. You can’t calm someone else’s tank for them, and pouring yours into theirs leaves two empty tanks. Protect yours: rest, say “later,” and give energy where it’s met. When both tanks are full, the kindest thing you control is the timing. More in Part One: who you are today (page 39)

Monday morning

You both look at the same pile of mail on the table. One of you sees a to-do list. The other sees proof that nobody else ever opens the mail. Same pile. Two different pictures.

Words this chapter uses

  • Stress tank: how much stress you are already carrying, before this moment even starts.
  • Leftover stress: the part of a feeling you brought in from somewhere else, like poor sleep or a hard day.
  • This-moment stress: the part caused by what is in front of you right now.
  • Angle: the point of view you are seeing a moment from, like tiredness or fairness.
  • How much are you carrying?: a free one-minute worksheet that scores your stress tank.
  • Calm-Down Kit: a short plan for stepping away well and coming back.

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Know how full your stress tank is, and which angle you are seeing from, before you judge a moment.
  • Between you and others: Choose the timing, pause and come back. Your state shapes how the other person’s words land, so say it out loud, and ask which angle they are seeing from.

On your own: reading your own tank

A full tank makes small things feel big. On your own, the most useful habit is a one-minute reading of your battery before you react.

  • Check your battery for a few mornings in a row and look for a pattern.
  • Before a hard moment, ask yourself how much of this is leftover from earlier.
  • Decide on a calm day what settles you, so it’s ready when you need it.

For example: Living alone after a breakup, Bryony noticed she snapped at her sister every Monday. Her mornings showed why: Sunday nights were her worst sleep of the week. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Words you could use: “Mondays are hard for me. Can we talk on Tuesday instead?”

In the individual program: Step 1: check your battery (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Step 4: plan what settles you · Part One: what settles you (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now-in-depth) · The whole book on staying calm (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-calm)

The fields behind this chapter

This chapter draws on 6 of the author’s thirteen fields (see the Preface (page 74) or the About page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/about)):

  • Neurobiology (Read your state first): The autonomic nervous system runs stress and rest without asking you.
  • Psychology (Tune how you send and receive): Leftover stress versus this-moment stress, family scripts and communication styles: the angles you see a moment from.
  • Philosophy (Tune how you send and receive): Two true views of the same thing (the Blind Men and the Elephant), and the Second Arrow: what happened is the first arrow, and the story we add is the second.
  • Holistic therapies (Read your state first): Body first, argument second.
  • Behavioural science (Read your state first): Say it before the talk, with a named time to come back. Practise small routines on calm days.
  • Economics (See the whole load): A tank that’s nearly full has no room to spare.

Two fields, one idea: Philosophy + Neurobiology. What happened is the first arrow. The story we add is the second. A full stress tank makes that second arrow easier to add, so say your tank and your angle out loud first.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

In real life

  • Partners: After a bad night’s sleep, “What’s for dinner?” sounds like “Why haven’t you taken care of dinner?”
  • Family: A parent asks about your job search. They see it from the angle of worry. You see it from the angle of an old pattern: “They’ve never trusted me.”
  • Roommates: Loud music at 11pm. One roommate sees it as a fairness issue. The other grew up in a noisy house and honestly didn’t notice.
  • Coworkers: A late-night email. The sender was clearing their inbox. The reader, who is already stretched, feels pressure to answer right away.
  • Two mums: One comes home from a hard shift to a toddler’s meltdown. Her “I can’t do this” is about the shift, not the toddler or her wife. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).
  • More than two partners: In a home of three, a check-in round where everyone says their tank first stops two people guessing about the third. See More than two (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).
  • Foster and kinship carers: After a contact visit, a child’s tank is often full. A slammed door that evening may be about the visit, not the carer. See Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).
  • A child with ADHD: The end of a school day can leave the tank brim full. Big talks go better after food and rest. See When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids).
  • Two faiths: A festival can mean joy to one partner and pressure to the other. Same day, two angles. See Two faiths, one family (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths).
  • Coming out: A parent’s silence may be shock, not rejection. Your own tank may be full for weeks afterwards. See Coming out (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-out).

Words you could use: “I think my tank was full before you walked in. Can we start again?”

Common mix-ups

  • “A big reaction means it was a big deal.” Sometimes. Often it means the tank was already full.
  • “A high score is an excuse.” It’s a note to come back later, not a pass to skip the talk.
  • “I can tell how full their tank is.” Only they can say. Each person scores only themselves.
  • “Pausing is the same as the silent treatment.” A pause has a time to come back. The silent treatment doesn’t. Always say when.
  • “If we see it differently, one of us is wrong.” You may just be standing at different angles.
  • “Naming my angle means giving up my point.” It just helps the other person see where your point is coming from.

Words you could use: “I don’t think you’re wrong. I think we’re standing in different places. Can we swap for a minute?”

zqaxchapterx3xxtwoxhomesqzTwo homes: co-parenting after a split

Children carry two homes, and changeover day fills their tank. Being quiet, clingy or cross for a few hours after a handover is common. It usually isn’t a sign that something is wrong at the other home.

  • Landing time: a snack, something familiar, and no questions about the other home for the first hour.
  • The child is never the messenger. Adult news goes adult to adult.
  • Money: follow any formal arrangement. Split the extras by a ratio you agree, keep one list, and settle up once a month.
  • With an ex, share the band, not the story: “I’m in a heavy week. Could we swap Wednesday?” Your private life stays yours.
  • An ex who won’t cooperate but isn’t dangerous: try parallel parenting. Written messages only, short and business-like, handovers at school, and your own list for your own home.
  • New partners: the parent stays the owner of anything involving the other home. A step-parent starts as a friendly adult, not the one who tells the children off.

For example (made up): Harriet gives Freya, 8, and Arlo, 5, an hour of toast and blankets when they come back from their dad’s. She stopped asking “What happened at Dad’s?” at the door. Sunday evenings got calmer.

Words you could use (a business-like message): “Hi Dylan. Freya’s school trip is on 6 November and costs £24. I’ve paid it and put it on the extras list. Thanks, Harriet.”

If you are afraid of your ex, a shared plan isn’t the right tool: see Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) Dig deeper: two homes, money and step-parents

If only one of you wants to try this

You can do all of this on your own side. Check your own tank. Name your own angle. Pause and come back on time. The other person doesn’t have to use the words for it to help. Often, when one person starts saying it out loud, the other starts to as well.

For example: A daughter visits her dad every Sunday, and every week they clash over his health. She starts each visit with “I’m a bit tired today, so if I go quiet, it’s not you.” He never scores anything. The visits still get calmer.

Words you could use: “I’ve been trying something. I just tell you how my day was before we talk about the hard stuff.”

Try this: Start your next hard talk with one sentence about your own tank, and nothing about theirs.

A note on safety: A full tank explains a reaction. It never excuses shouting, threats or hurting anyone. If someone’s “stress” often turns into fear for you, that isn’t a tank problem. These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If sharing how you feel ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? lists free, private hotlines.

More for your situation

Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room) · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

Try this: Before your next hard conversation, check how full your own tank is.

Score the five things in How much are you carrying?, add them up and divide by 20.

Then say one sentence out loud, such as: “My stress tank’s about half full today, and I’m mostly seeing this from the time-pressure angle.”

If either of you scores 0.60 or more, put off anything that doesn’t need deciding in the next hour. Agree on a time to come back, and keep it.

Today’s Weather, a one-minute self-check → How much are you carrying? → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying) See it from their side → The Calm-Down Kit →

What to remember

  • A full tank overflows. Stress left over from earlier makes small things feel big.
  • Check your tank in a minute, and say the band out loud instead of making others guess.
  • Two people can see one moment from different angles, and both views can be true.
  • A full tank means “later,” not “never”: pause, name a time, and come back.
