IV

Part Two · Chapter IV

Two kinds of fair: equal vs fair at home

Agree on what “fair” means before you argue about it, and give a comment a moment to land before you answer it.

In this chapter

  1. There are two kinds of fair
  2. Fair by results
  3. Fair by promises
  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner
  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud
  6. Let a comment land before you react
  7. Notice, name, decide
  8. Keep the two questions apart
  9. Each idea in everyday life
  10. Inside you, and between you
  11. On your own: your own kind of fair
  12. The fields behind this chapter
  13. In real life
  14. Common mix-ups
  15. Money between you
  16. A couple and a housemate
  17. More for your situation
  18. A note on safety

In short:

  • There are two kinds of fair: by results (did it all get done?) and by promises (did each of us do what we agreed?). Agree which one you’re using.
  • Once a job has an owner, look to the owner. Covering for someone is kind when you say it out loud.
  • Let a comment land before you react: notice it, name it, then decide what to say.
  • Keep the two questions apart: “Was the job done?” is about a fact; “Did that comment hurt?” is about a feeling.

The big ideas: This chapter mostly teaches “Fix the setup, not the person” and “Notice the quiet incentives”, with help from “Read your state first”. What are the five big ideas?

The same argument, twice a month

One of you counts hours. The other counts who noticed the job needed doing. You’re both counting honestly, in two different currencies, and then arguing about the exchange rate.

  1. There are two kinds of fair.

    “Did everything get done?” and “Did each of us do what we said we’d do?” Both are reasonable. Friction starts when each of you is using a different one without realising.

    Dig deeper: the two kinds of fair

  2. Fair by results.

    This kind judges by outcomes: did the right things get done, by whoever had the time or energy? It’s flexible and easy-going. Done carefully, it counts the cost to whoever covered, but done carelessly, it can hide who is always stepping in.

    Dig deeper: judging by results

  3. Fair by promises.

    This kind asks whether each person did the jobs they agreed to own. It’s clear and steady, but it can feel rigid in a week when life gets in the way.

    Dig deeper: judging by promises

  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner.

    The owner is the person who does the job, start to finish. A second name on the list is a backstop who notices if it slipped and gently checks in, never a supervisor. (It can be the same person.) If it’s your job, the question is whether you did it, not whether someone else quietly covered for you. That protects the person who keeps filling the gaps.

    Dig deeper: agreeing which kind you’ll use

  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud.

    Helping out when the owner can’t is lovely. Just mention it, so the help is seen: “I put the bins out this week, since you were away.” Help that stays silent turns into unseen work, and unseen help slowly becomes expected (see Complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency)).

    Dig deeper: covering without resentment

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: covering for someone is kind. Say it out loud, gently, and ask for what you’d like next time, so it doesn’t turn into quiet resentment.

    Tool: Turn a complaint into a request spreadloveandacceptance.com/small-wins

  6. Let a comment land before you react.

    When a remark hits harder than it should, say “Give me a second.” The idea is borrowed loosely from brain science, where the brain turns down sounds and sensations automatically, in a fraction of a second. This book’s pause is different: a few seconds you choose to take on purpose. Let the spike pass, then decide whether it needs an answer now, later or not at all.

    Dig deeper: giving a comment time to land

  7. Notice, name, decide.

    Notice it landed hard. Name it kindly: “That hit harder than you probably meant.” Then, once you’ve settled, decide how to reply. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps with the words.

    Dig deeper: the three steps

  8. Keep the two questions apart.

    “Was the job done?” is a question about a fact. “Did that comment hurt?” is a question about a feeling. Both matter. Answer them one at a time, not in the same argument.

    Dig deeper: facts and feelings, separately

Each idea in everyday life

The sections above say what each idea means. Here each one gets a real-life example, words you could say, and one small step.

zqaxchapterx4xxextwoxkindsqz1. Two kinds of fair

For example: Nisha and Kezia share a dorm room. Nisha thinks it’s fair if the room is tidy by Friday, whoever tidies. Kezia thinks it’s fair if each keeps their own half clean. See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).

Words you could use: “When you say fair, do you mean it all gets done, or that we each do our bit?”

Try this: Each finish this sentence, then compare: “To me, a fair week is one where…”

2. Fair by results

For example: A grandmother is raising her grandchildren. Her grown-up son helps “wherever it’s needed” when he’s home. The house runs, but she is always the one who notices what’s needed. See Kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).

Words you could use: “I like that we’re flexible. Can we also check who ends up stepping in most?”

Try this: For one week, mark every job you picked up that wasn’t planned.

3. Fair by promises

For example: Two business partners run a café. One owns the ordering, the other the staff rota. When the rota is late, they ask the rota owner, not “the team.”

Words you could use: “It’s my job, and I can’t do it this week. Could you take it, and I’ll take the bins?”

Try this: Name one job that is “sort of everyone’s.” Agree who owns it for a month.

zqaxchapterx4xxexownerqz4. Look to the owner

For example: In a stepfamily, the 13-year-old owns feeding the dog, and his stepmum is the second name. At 7pm the bowl is empty. She says, “Dog’s dinner?” once. She doesn’t do it for him, and she doesn’t lecture.

Words you could use: “This one’s yours, start to finish. I’ll only remind you if it slips.”

Try this: Pick one job that causes friction and write two names next to it.

5. Covering out loud

For example: Two grown-up sisters take turns driving their dad to appointments. When one covers, she texts: “I took Dad Thursday since you had the late shift. Just so you know.”

Words you could use: “Thank you for covering that. How was it for you?”

Try this: Next time you cover a job, mention it in one plain sentence, the same day.

zqaxchapterx4xxexlandqz6. Let a comment land

For example: A nurse comes home from a night shift. Her husband says, “Oh, you’re up.” She hears “at last,” but says, “Give me a second, I’m very tired.” He meant he was glad to see her. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

Words you could use: “That landed hard. Let me think before I answer.”

Try this: Agree on your “give me a second” phrase today, on a calm day.

Professor Puddles

When a comment stings, give it a minute to land before you answer. This workpaper is a short check for your reply.

Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

7. Notice, name, decide

For example: A teenager tells her dad, “You never listen.” He feels his chest tighten (notice). He says, “That stings, and I want to hear you properly” (name). He decides it needs a real talk tomorrow (decide). See Teens (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens).

Words you could use: “I want to answer that, just not this minute. Can we talk at eight?”

Try this: Put the three words somewhere you’ll see them, like the fridge.

8. Keep the two questions apart

For example: Separated parents share the kids across two homes. The bag came back without the school shoes (a fact). The text about it felt cold (a feeling). They sort the shoes first. See Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

Words you could use: “Can we sort the shoes first, and come back to how that text felt?”

Try this: When a talk tangles, ask, “Fact or feeling?” and finish one first.

Your part, and only your part. You control whether, when and how you bring something up, and whether you cover a job out loud. How the other person responds is theirs. If you cover again and again with no thanks and no change, match the energy: cover less, and say so kindly. Fair by promises only works when both people keep theirs. More in Part One: who you are today (page 39)

The weekly catch-up

Sam and Alex share a home. Alex owns the bins, but Alex works late on Tuesdays, and Sam has quietly taken it out three weeks running. At the catch-up, Sam mentions it. Alex says Tuesday nights aren’t realistic with the late shifts. They agree to try a swap for the rest of the month: Sam takes the bins, and Alex takes the recycling and the weekly grocery order. They’ll settle it at the monthly look-back in Chapter V (page 172).

Wednesday, 7pm

“Thanks for doing the dishes,” one of you says, a little flatly. It was meant as a thank-you. It sounded like a criticism. Before you know it, you’ve replied to the criticism, and now there really is one.

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Notice which kind of fair comes naturally to you, and notice the quiet habit of covering for others without saying so. When a comment stings, check your own state before you answer.
  • Between you and others: Give each job one clear owner instead of blaming. Watch how unowned jobs slide towards one person, and keep things steady by mentioning help out loud and saying thank you.

On your own: your own kind of fair

Fair starts with knowing what fair means to you, and which jobs are truly yours.

  • Write down what fair means to you, in one sentence.
  • List the jobs you own, and the ones you picked up without ever agreeing.
  • Practise letting a comment land before you answer, then reply with a fact, a feeling and an ask.

For example: Olu lives alone and has his kids every other weekend. His line: “Fair is not doing their jobs just because I miss them.” See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Try this: Pick one job you took on without agreeing. Keep it on purpose, or raise it on a calm day.

In the individual program: Step 5: find words for what you feel (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Step 6: kind ways to say no · Part One: where your sense of fair came from (page 22) · The whole book on sharing the load (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-share-the-load)

The fields behind this chapter

This chapter draws on 6 of the author’s thirteen fields (see the Preface (page 74) or the About page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/about)).

  • Philosophy (Fix the setup, not the person): Two old ideas behind fairness: judging by outcomes (consequentialist) and judging by promises (deontological).
  • Business (Fix the setup, not the person): Look to the owner.
  • Economics (Notice the quiet incentives): Two people keeping score in two currencies, then arguing about the exchange rate.
  • Neurobiology (Read your state first): How the brain turns down sounds and sensations, borrowed loosely. In the brain it is automatic and takes a fraction of a second; here it’s a few seconds you choose to take.
  • Aromatherapy (Read your state first): For some people, a familiar scent or a calmer room is a quick cue to slow down. Where and when you talk is part of the method.
  • Psychology (Notice the quiet incentives): Why a flat “thanks” can be heard as sarcasm, and why covering turns sour only when it’s silent.

Two fields, one idea: Philosophy + Business. People can mean two different things by “fair.” A job list with one owner per job makes it simple: check the job, not the person.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

In real life

  • Partners: One counts hours spent cleaning. The other counts all the planning that happened before anyone picked up a cloth. Both are real work, so put the planning on the list too, in minutes.
  • Parents: Older kids can own age-sized jobs too, like feeding the cat or packing their own lunch. Put their name on the list, with a parent as the second name.
  • Family: One sibling visits a parent every week. Another pays for extra help. Each thinks they’re doing their share, in a different currency.
  • Roommates: One wants a fixed schedule. The other prefers “whoever’s free does it.” Neither is lazy. They just use different kinds of fair.
  • Coworkers: One person quietly fixes everyone else’s slides before the meeting. Because it always gets done, nobody knows it was ever a problem.
  • More than two partners: In a home with three adults, the one who works from home is always the one who “can.” See More than two (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).
  • Different hours: Someone who works nights sleeps in the day. Being home isn’t being free. See Different hours.
  • When one is ill: Share by energy, not hours, with a backup agreed for low days. See When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).
  • Friends: One friend always hosts, and nobody thanks them anymore. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).

Words you could use: “I think we’re counting in different ways. Can we put both on the list?”

Try this: Read the example closest to your home to the other person, and ask, “Does this sound like us?”

Common mix-ups

  • “If it got done, there’s no problem.” Someone may be paying for that in time and energy.
  • “Holding the owner to it is being strict.” It’s just keeping the agreement you both made. That’s kinder than quiet resentment.
  • “Letting a comment land means ignoring it.” It’s about timing, not about swallowing your feelings.
  • “‘Give me a second’ is rude.” It’s a way of taking the other person seriously enough to answer well.
  • “One kind of fair is the right one.” Both are reasonable. What matters is agreeing which one you’ll use.
  • “The owner is the boss of that job.” The owner does the job. They don’t direct everyone else, and the second name isn’t a supervisor.
  • “I covered for months, so now I can bring it all up.” A long list lands as a bill. Mention covering as it happens.

Words you could use: “I don’t think either of us is wrong. I think we’ve been using different rulers.”

zqaxchapterx4xxmoneyqzMoney between you

Money is where the two kinds of fair meet most often. Three common ways to share it:

  • All shared: both incomes go into one pot.
  • Separate: each keeps their own money and pays agreed bills, often half each. That’s fair by promises: the same rule for both.
  • Proportional: each puts into a shared pot in line with what they earn, and keeps the rest. That’s fair by results: each is left with a similar share.

Many couples mix them: a joint account for bills and food, and some money each that nobody has to explain. The right way is the one you both chose with your eyes open. To talk about it, start with your money stories (how money worked at home when you were growing up), then the numbers, then a “talk first” amount for big buys that applies to both of you. A limit you both chose and both keep is care, not control.

For example (made up): Niamh takes home £2,600 a month and Tariq £1,900. Rent and bills will be £1,500. They split it 58/42, in line with their pay: £870 and £630.

Words you could use: “Can we each say how money worked in our families growing up?” “Would half each, or in line with our pay, feel fairer to you?”

Dig deeper: money, step by step

zqaxchapterx4xxhousemateqzA couple and a housemate

A couple sharing a home with a housemate who isn’t a partner is a different shape from three equals. Keep two lists: house jobs for all three of you (bins, bathroom, bills, the landlord), and couple jobs just for the two of you. Decide house questions with all three of you there, not in bed the night before. Hear the housemate first on anything that affects them, keep couple arguments out of shared rooms, and never ask them to be the referee.

For example (made up): Ollie and Hamza share a flat with their friend Bex. They split the rent by room (the couple has the bigger one) and the bills by person. All three hold a short house meeting on the first Sunday of the month.

Words you could use: “That’s a house question. Let’s decide it when Bex is here.”

Dig deeper: two lists, and money with three

More for your situation

Each of these pages takes the ideas in this chapter into one kind of relationship. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists them all.

  • Friends · More than two partners · Sharing a room · Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together)
  • Foster and kinship families · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts)
  • Different hours · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one is ill · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own

Try this: Agree on what counts as fair on a calm, easy day, not in the middle of a disagreement.

Start by each saying which kind of fair comes more naturally to you: results or promises.

Then pick three regular jobs and write an owner for each in the job list: the person who does it. Add a second name, someone who notices if it slips. It can be the same person.

Finally, agree on a short phrase for when something lands hard, like “Give me a second.” Agree that the other person will wait, and that the person who asked for a second will come back to it.

Write it down: one owner per job → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job) Say it so it lands →

A note on safety

These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about what’s fair ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A promise is something both people chose and either can ask to change. Rules one person sets for the other, with checking, punishment or money held back, are control, and that is not your fault. See normal limits and control.

Words you could use, with someone you trust: “Things at home don’t feel fair, and I’m scared to bring it up. Can I talk it through with you?”

What to remember

  • There are two kinds of fair: by results (did it all get done?) and by promises (did each of us do what we agreed?). Agree which one you’re using.
  • Once a job has an owner, look to the owner. Covering for someone is kind when you say it out loud.
  • Let a comment land before you react: notice it, name it, then decide what to say.
  • Keep the two questions apart: “Was the job done?” is about a fact; “Did that comment hurt?” is about a feeling.

V

Part Two · Chapter V

The monthly look-back: a calm relationship check-in

Once a month, look back for the problems that keep coming back, and fix the setup instead of having the same argument again.

In this chapter

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns
  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list
  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped
  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner
  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds
  6. Count the gaps each month
  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping
  8. It’s not a review of either person
  9. Keep it short and kind
  10. Each idea in everyday life
  11. Inside you, and between you
  12. In real life
  13. Common mix-ups
  14. Starting out: before you move in
  15. Raising a grandchild (kinship care)
  16. More for your situation
  17. On your own: a monthly look at yourself
  18. The fields behind this chapter

In short:

  • Weekly check-ins miss patterns. Once a month, look back over four weeks of notes and your job list.
  • Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped. Anything with two or more gets sorted.
  • A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner. Fix the setup, not the person.
  • Keep it short and kind, and look back even in the quiet months.

The big ideas: This chapter mostly teaches “Fix the setup, not the person” and “Notice the quiet incentives”, with help from “See the whole load”. What are the five big ideas?

The third Tuesday in a row

The bins again. You could have the same ten-minute back-and-forth about Tuesday. Or you could notice that Tuesday has now happened three times, and ask what it is about Tuesdays.

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns.

    One missed job looks like bad luck. The same job missed week after week is a pattern, and it’s easiest to see when you look at the whole month. The “audit” here is a careful, friendly look back, more like a self-check than an inspection.

    Dig deeper: why once a month

  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list.

    Bring the month’s four weekly notes from Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01) (a few lines a week is enough) and your job list from One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job). That’s all. Twenty minutes is usually enough. If either of your stress tanks is high that day (0.60 or more on How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying)), move it a day or two.

    Dig deeper: getting ready

  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped.

    A job “slipped” if it was noticed but not done, only done after being raised more than once, or quietly covered by someone who isn’t its owner. Look closely at every job with two or more ✗. Three or four in a month is a real pattern, not just bad luck.

    Dig deeper: gathering the month’s notes

  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner.

    It gets patched every week and never fixed. The owner is the person who does the job, start to finish. The fix is to give the job one owner whose name sticks, or to talk honestly about whether anyone has the time and energy for it.

    Dig deeper: spotting the gaps that keep reopening

  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds.

    No clear owner: update the job list. An owner who can’t keep up: have a kind, honest talk. A short-term cause, like illness or travel: note it and move on.

    Dig deeper: sorting each gap

  6. Count the gaps each month.

    Write down how many gaps of each kind you found. If the number of jobs with no clear owner falls over several months, the setup is working; one month can be a normal swing. If it keeps rising, something bigger has changed, and it’s worth a talk.

    Dig deeper: keeping count

    Professor Puddles

    The look-back has its own workpaper: a month of notes, one list, and an ✗ for each week a job slipped. It makes a pattern easy to see.

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping.

    A month with no gaps is good news, and it’s also the month most likely to go unchecked. When something has worked for a while, people stop looking, and nothing breaks on the day that happens. Keep the look-back going on quiet months, and add one question: “What’s something we’ve stopped noticing or mentioning?” That is how a look-back guards against complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency).

    Dig deeper: the quiet months

  8. It’s not a review of either person.

    You don’t add up old hours or punish old mistakes. You can thank someone for what they carried before; you just don’t bill for the past. The only question is where the setup isn’t working yet, and what you’ll try next month.

    Dig deeper: what the look-back is for, and what it isn’t

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: a look-back can start with a high five. Name one thing that went well first! The weekly card has a nice way to begin.

    Tool: Weekly check-in card spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins

  9. Keep it short and kind.

    Start with something that went well. Talk about the job, not the person. If a gap needs a proper talk, set it for another day using Check-ins (spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins). If a talk starts going badly, either of you can call a pause, and the person who paused names a time to come back.

    Dig deeper: how to talk about a pattern

Each idea in everyday life

The sections above say what each idea means. Here each one gets a real-life example, words you could say, and one small step.

1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns

For example: Four flatmates. Each week the bathroom bin overflowed, and each week it looked like bad luck. Looking at the whole month showed it happened every single week.

Words you could use: “Can we look at the whole month, not just this week?”

Try this: Pick a monthly date now, like the last Sunday, and put it in both calendars.

2. Four weeks of notes and one list

For example: A couple on different shifts keep their weekly notes in one shared note on their phones. They do the look-back on the one evening they’re both off. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

Words you could use: “I’m running on empty today. Can we move the look-back to Thursday?”

Try this: Choose one place where both of you can find the weekly notes.

3. Mark an ✗ when a job slipped

For example: Two foster carers look back. The reading log was missed three weeks out of four. Three ✗ means it’s a pattern, not a bad week. See Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).

Words you could use: “This isn’t about who. It’s just which jobs slipped.”

Try this: Mark the ✗ in pencil, together, before anyone explains anything.

zqaxchapterx5xxexnoxownerqz4. A repeat usually has no real owner

For example: Three partners share a home. “Whoever’s free” does the grocery order, and it was late three times. Nobody owned it, so everybody assumed. See More than two (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).

Words you could use: “Whose name is next to this one? If nobody’s, shall we pick?”

Try this: For each job with two or more ✗, check that one name is written next to it.

5. Sort each repeat

For example: Separated parents look at the missed homework folder. Was nobody sure which home signs it (no owner)? Is one parent swamped (can’t keep up)? Or was it the week she had flu (a one-off)? See Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

Words you could use: “Is this a list problem, a too-much problem, or just a bad week?”

Try this: Write one of the three kinds next to every repeat before you decide what to do.

6. Count the gaps

For example: Two business partners write their monthly count on a whiteboard in the back office. In March, four jobs had no clear owner. By June, one did.

Words you could use: “Let’s just write the numbers down and see how they look in three months.”

Try this: Write this month’s three numbers on the back page of your notes.

7. Look back on quiet months too

For example: The kids have left home and nothing is slipping. At the look-back, one of them says, “We don’t really talk at dinner anymore.” Nothing was broken. Something was drifting. See Kids grown and gone (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest).

Words you could use: “What’s something we’ve stopped noticing or mentioning?”

Try this: Keep the date on a quiet month, and ask just that one question.

8. Not a review of either person

For example: After a month in hospital, one partner comes home to a long list of what slipped. They thank each other for what each carried instead, and fix only next month. See When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

Words you could use: “I see how much you carried. Let’s just set up next month.”

Try this: If you notice yourself adding up past hours, stop and say one thank-you instead.

9. Short and kind

For example: A mum and two teens hold their look-back over pizza. Each says one good thing first. One gap gets a new owner. It’s over in fifteen minutes. See Teens (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens).

Words you could use: “This needs a proper talk. Can we do it Thursday, not now?”

Try this: Set a timer for twenty minutes, and stop when it rings.

Your part, and only your part. In the look-back you can only fix the gaps you own, and offer help with the rest. You can’t make someone keep a rhythm. Keep the rhythms you can keep, notice which ones are kept in return, and let your effort follow: more where it’s shared, less where it isn’t, so the rhythm doesn’t run on one person’s energy. More in Part One: who you are today (page 39)

The last Sunday of the month

Two mugs of tea, four weeks of notes and twenty minutes. You go down the list. Most weeks went fine. Two jobs keep coming up. That’s the whole meeting, and it’s enough.

Inside you, and between you

  • In you: Look at your own routines as a setup you can adjust. Spot the easy defaults, like “I’ll just do it,” that let a gap quietly reopen.
  • Between you and others: Look at the month together, give repeating gaps a clear owner, and keep count so jobs don’t drift back to whoever notices first.

In real life

  • Partners: Sam and Alex’s bins slipped three weeks in a row, because Alex works late on Tuesdays. After a trial swap, they make it official: Sam owns the bins, and Alex takes the recycling and the weekly grocery order, so the hours stay even.
  • Family: Three siblings keep forgetting to call their dad’s landlord about repairs. It turns out nobody ever agreed who would.
  • Roommates: The recycling overflows every other week. Everyone thought someone else was taking it down.
  • Coworkers: Meeting notes go missing twice a month. Giving note-taking a named owner fixes it by the next month.
  • Long distance: A couple in two cities do the look-back by video. Their repeat is “who calls first,” so they give it an owner per weekday. See Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance).
  • Friends: Two friends notice their monthly dinner has been cancelled three times. Nobody owned booking it. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • Grandparents and parents: School pick-ups by grandma slipped twice, both on days she wasn’t told about. The gap was the message, not grandma. See Grandparents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grandparents).

Words you could use: “I don’t think anyone dropped this. I think nobody ever picked it up.”

Common mix-ups

  • “This is where we settle who owes what.” Past hours are never billed to anyone, though you can still say thank you for them. You only fix the setup going forward.
  • “If a job slipped, the owner failed.” The gap might be in the list, in the owner’s capacity, or just a one-off week.
  • “One bad week means we should change everything.” Don’t make a lasting change because of a short-term cause.
  • “We can skip the weekly checks and just do this.” The monthly look-back only works if the weekly notes feed it.
  • “More gaps this month means we’re failing.” One month can be a normal swing, or it can mean life changed. That’s a reason to talk, not to worry.
  • “The look-back is for the person who keeps the notes.” It works best when both bring their notes, and both talk.

A note on safety: These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If looking back together ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A look-back is something you both choose. If one person demands logs of the other’s every hour, checks their phone without agreement, or uses the ✗ marks to punish, that is control, not a look-back, and it is not your fault. See Not safe at home? and normal limits and control (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together).

zqaxchapterx5xxmovingxinqzStarting out: before you move in

New together, and about to share a home? The tools work best now, before habits set. A gentle order, about one step a week:

  1. Week 1: each write down the rulebook from the home you grew up in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up), then swap. Be curious, not judging.
  2. Week 2: talk about money: your money stories first, then the split (Chapter IV (page 168)).
  3. Week 3: write your first job list, with one owner per job, thinking jobs included (One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-03)).
  4. Week 4: make a pause plan (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) on a calm day.
  5. Week 5: each name three things that matter most to you about a home (Part Three, Chapter 10 (page 335)).
  6. After the move: log one ordinary week after two weeks, and do your first short look-back after four.

It isn’t a test, and it isn’t keeping score. It’s so neither of you has to guess.

For example (made up): Niamh and Tariq, eight months together, find their families meant different things by “tidy.” They agree: kitchen every night, the rest on Sunday.

Words you could use: “I don’t want us to keep score. I just want us never to have to guess. Could we try a few small things before we move?”

Dig deeper: the plan, week by week

zqaxchapterx5xxkinshipqzRaising a grandchild (kinship care)

Many grandparents and other relatives raise a child whose parents can’t, and much of it is about things that keep coming back: cancelled calls, hard evenings after contact, forms. A monthly look-back helps. Some repeats you can own; some, like a parent who misses calls, you can’t. For those, own the plan for the evening after.

  • The loyalty bind: the child may love the parent who can’t look after them and you. Tell them they don’t have to choose, and don’t run the parent down in front of them.
  • Explaining an absent parent: short, true and kind, in words for their age, and always “it’s not your fault.”
  • When the parent is your own adult child and things are hard between you: keep messages about the child short and civil, for the child’s sake, and leave the door open.
  • Look after yourself: ask for respite and join other kinship carers. In England and Wales, the charity Kinship (kinship.org.uk) can help.

For example (made up): Maureen, 63, is raising her grandson Tyler, 9. Her look-back shows his mum’s Sunday call fell through three times this month. She plans those evenings (hot chocolate, his football annual) and asks her brother to take Tyler swimming on Sunday afternoons.

Words you could use, with the child: “Mum loves you. She isn’t well enough to look after you right now, and that’s not your fault.”

Dig deeper: loyalty, explaining by age, and rifts with your adult child

More for your situation

A look-back works in every kind of relationship, with small changes. These pages take it into one situation each. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists them all.

  • More than two partners · Money together · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room)
  • Foster and kinship families · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Kids grown and gone
  • Different hours · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one is ill · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

On your own: a monthly look at yourself

Once a month, look back at your own month, kindly. Not a scorecard, more like a weather report.

  • What filled your battery this month, and what drained it?
  • Which of your limits held, and which slipped?
  • Choose one small thing to keep, and one to change next month.

For example: Gillian lives on her own after a divorce. Her monthly look-back shows the same ✗ three weeks running: she skipped her Thursday swim to answer work emails. She moves the emails, not the swim. See On my own.

Words you could use (to yourself): “Not a scorecard. Just this month’s weather.”

Try this: On the last day of this month, write three lines: one thing that filled you, one that drained you, one thing to change.

In the individual program: The Individual package and your report (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Part One: a kind monthly look at yourself (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-3-next-in-depth) · Step 1: check your battery · The whole book on sharing the load (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-share-the-load)

The fields behind this chapter

This chapter draws on 7 of the author’s thirteen fields (see the Preface (page 74) or the About page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/about)):

  • Finance (See the whole load): The month-end close: check the plan against the log, so next month starts clean.
  • Business (Fix the setup, not the person): The audit habit, as a friendly self-check. A job that keeps slipping usually has no real owner.
  • Economics (Notice the quiet incentives): Past hours can’t be handed back, so they aren’t billed.
  • Behavioural science (Notice the quiet incentives): Three or four slips in a month is a pattern that’s easy to miss week by week.
  • Psychology (Tune how you send and receive): Say a pattern as a repeated fact, not a verdict.
  • Philosophy (Fix the setup, not the person): The Ship of Theseus: a ship rebuilt plank by plank is still the same ship. Your agreements can be rebuilt and still be yours.
  • Holistic therapies (Read your state first): Body first, argument second. A calm look-back a few days late beats a tense one on time.

Two fields, one idea: Finance + Business. Once a month, look back like an audit: which jobs kept slipping? A job that keeps slipping usually needs an owner, not more effort.

See how all the fields connect, in the full version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-5-in-depth) · The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath)

Try this: Put a relaxed 20-minute date on the calendar, once a month.

Until then, keep your weekly Who did what notes somewhere you can both find them.

At the look-back, start by naming one thing that went well this month.

End by writing down how many gaps of each kind you found, so over the next few months you can see if the number is falling.

Use the monthly look-back for that conversation → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-04-what-keeps-coming-back) Keep the count month by month → (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/report-01)

That’s the end of Part Two. The book goes on in Part Three: Understanding people (page 194), chapters on how people work, for anyone. To put Parts One and Two into practice first, try the six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01): six gentle weeks, with one chapter and one small tool each week.

What to remember

  • Weekly check-ins miss patterns. Once a month, look back over four weeks of notes and your job list.
  • Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped. Anything with two or more gets sorted.
  • A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner. Fix the setup, not the person.
  • Keep it short and kind, and look back even in the quiet months.

Part Three · Chapter 1

How feelings work: signals, the body, and naming what you feel

What feelings are for, where they start, and why putting a name to one can make it easier to carry. For anyone: on your own, at home, with friends, at work or out in the world.

In this chapter

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict
  2. Feelings start in the body
  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it
  4. More words, better tools
  5. Feelings come in layers
  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves
  7. Feelings spread between people
  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings
  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short:

  • A feeling is a signal, not a verdict. It says “something here matters to me.” It doesn’t say what to do.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often comes before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • Feeling it isn’t doing it. You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • Today’s Weather and the daily check-in (Part One, Now (page 39); Part Two, Chapter I (page 93)) ask for one word about how you are. Naming a feeling turns its volume down a little, and a daily word catches feelings while they are still small. Big idea: read your state first.
  • Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV (page 151)) asks for a feeling, not a verdict. “I felt let down” is easier to hear than “you never care.” Big idea: tune how you send and receive.

Thursday, 4:50pm

A message from your manager: “Got a minute tomorrow?” Your stomach drops. By the time you get home you have snapped at the cat, skipped dinner and replayed every mistake from the last month. Nobody has said anything bad. Your body heard “trouble” before you had a single clear thought.

This part of the book is about how people work: you, and everyone around you. We start with feelings, because they are under almost everything else. How we talk, how we see each other and how we handle stress all run through them. This chapter teaches how feelings work first. What to do with them comes second.

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict.

    Feelings are fast messages about what matters to you. Fear says “something might be a danger.” Anger says “something seems unfair, or in my way.” Sadness says “I lost something that mattered.” A signal is worth listening to. But it can be wrong about the details, the way a smoke alarm can go off for burnt toast.

    For example: You feel jealous when a friend makes a new close friend. The jealousy isn’t proof that you’re a bad person, or that your friend is leaving. It is a signal that the friendship matters to you.

    Thoughts you could try: “This feeling is telling me something matters. What is it?” “Is this the fire, or the toast?”

    Try this: Next time a strong feeling arrives, finish this sentence: “This feeling is trying to protect…”

    Dig deeper: what feelings are for

  2. Feelings start in the body.

    Often your body reacts before your mind has a word: a racing heart, a hot face, a heavy chest, a knot in the stomach. Your brain then tries to make sense of it. That’s why being hungry, tired or in pain can feel a lot like being upset. The body is sending a strong signal, and the mind guesses what it means.

    For example: A teenager comes home “furious” at their parent over nothing much. After a sandwich and a sit-down, the fury is mostly gone. Some of it was hunger wearing anger’s coat.

    Thoughts you could try: “Where is this in my body?” “Am I hungry, tired, cold or sore right now?”

    Try this: Three times today, pause and ask: “What does my body feel like right now?” Just notice. No need to change anything.

    Dig deeper: the body and the brain’s best guess

  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it.

    Putting a feeling into words can turn its volume down a little. In brain-scan research by Lieberman and colleagues (2007), simply putting a name to a feeling (“I feel scared”) turned down the brain’s alarm response. A name gives a big, cloudy rush some edges, so you can see it, talk about it and decide what to do.

    For example: Two housemates are tense all evening. One finally says, “I think I’m embarrassed about the noise complaint, and I’ve been acting cross.” The other relaxes. Now they know what’s in the room.

    Words you could use: “I think what I’m feeling is…” “I’m not sure what this is yet. Maybe worried?”

    Try this: Once a day, name one feeling out loud or on paper. A guess is fine. “Something like sad” still counts.

    Dig deeper: why naming works

    Professor Puddles

    If the words won’t come, weather words often will. Pick “foggy” or “stormy” and start from there.

    Tool: How am I right now? A mood and energy check spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  4. More words, better tools.

    “Bad” is a very blunt word. “Disappointed,” “left out,” “overwhelmed” and “ashamed” each point to something different, and each needs something different. A review by Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight (2015) found that people who can tell their feelings apart more finely tend to cope with them in healthier ways. You don’t need fancy words. You can use numbers, colours or body words too.

    For example: A dad tells his partner, “I feel bad about my mum.” They talk in circles. Then he says, “Actually, I feel guilty that I haven’t visited, and scared she’s getting worse.” Now the talk has somewhere to go.

    Words you could use: “On a scale of one to ten, I’m about a six.” “It’s less angry and more… let down.” “It feels heavy, like a grey day.”

    Try this: When you notice “bad,” try for one more exact word. When you notice “fine,” try for one more honest one.

    Dig deeper: finer words, finer tools

  5. Feelings come in layers.

    The feeling you show first isn’t always the first one you felt. Anger is often a cover for hurt or fear, because anger feels stronger and safer. And we often have feelings about our feelings: ashamed of being sad, scared of being angry. That second layer can hurt more than the first.

    For example: A grandmother is short with her daughter after the grandkids’ visit is cancelled. Under the shortness is hurt. Under the hurt is a fear: “Am I still needed?”

    Thoughts you could try: “What might be under this one?” “It’s okay to feel this. I don’t also have to feel bad for feeling it.”

    Try this: Next time you feel angry, ask gently: “Is there hurt or worry underneath?” You don’t have to say it. Just look.

    Dig deeper: first feelings and feelings about feelings

  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves.

    Most feelings, even big ones, rise, peak and settle if you don’t keep feeding them. Moods are different. They are like weather (in plain words: a background feeling that lasts hours or days) that colours everything, often without you noticing. A grey mood can make a small thing feel huge, and a good mood can make the same thing feel like nothing.

    For example: A woman living alone has a bad morning and decides “my whole life is going nowhere.” By evening, after a walk and a call with her sister, the same life looks ordinary and okay. The facts didn’t change. Her weather did.

    Thoughts you could try: “This is a wave. It will peak and pass.” “Is this a feeling about now, or a mood colouring everything?”

    Try this: Don’t make big decisions at the top of a wave. Write the decision down, and look at it again tomorrow.

    Dig deeper: waves and weather

  7. Feelings spread between people.

    We pick up each other’s feelings, often without noticing: a tense voice, a sigh, a slammed door. That’s part of how people bond. It also means stress can move round a home or a team like a cold. You can care about someone’s feeling without catching all of it.

    For example: A team leader comes into a meeting rushed and anxious. Within ten minutes the whole team feels behind. The next week, she takes two slow breaths at the door first. The meeting feels different.

    Thoughts you could try: “Is this feeling mine, or did I pick it up?” “I can stay beside their storm without standing in the middle of it.”

    Try this: Notice who you tend to “catch” feelings from. Before your next talk with them, settle yourself for one minute first.

    Dig deeper: how feelings spread

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: good moods are catching too! Tail wags definitely are. Want a small way to share one?

    Tool: Get one small bonding idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings.

    Many people grew up in homes, generations or cultures where feelings were kept private: “Don’t make a fuss,” “Big boys don’t cry,” “We don’t talk about that.” This is common for men and for older people, and in some cultures it is a sign of respect and strength.

    It isn’t a flaw. And it doesn’t mean you don’t feel. Many people who rarely say a feeling show it every day by doing: fixing the tap, driving someone to hospital, turning up. Caring by doing is real caring. Words can be added slowly, at your own pace, a few at a time.

    For example: A retired builder whose wife has died has never talked about feelings in his life. At his grandson’s football match, he finally says to his son, “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her. Every morning.” His son puts a hand on his shoulder. Nothing else needs to be said.

    Words you could use: “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her.” “I’m not good with words for this. It’s been a hard week.” “I don’t know what to call it. I just feel heavy.” “I’m not one for talking, but I wanted you to know I’m proud of you.”

    Try this: Pick one sentence above and say it once this week, to one person, or even just out loud on your own. Short is fine. A text counts. So does writing it down.

    Dig deeper: when feelings weren’t talked about

  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it.

    A feeling usually comes with an urge: to shout, run, hide, check, fix or text. The feeling isn’t a choice. What you do with the urge is more of one. Pushing a feeling down tends to make it come back stronger, and acting on every urge can hurt people. The middle path is: let the feeling be there, and choose the action.

    For example: A father feels a hot rush of anger when his son breaks a window with a ball. He says, “I’m too cross to talk right now. Let’s sort this out in ten minutes.” The anger was real. The shouting didn’t happen.

    Words you could use: “I’m feeling a lot right now. I’m going to take a minute before I answer.” “I want to reply when I’m calmer.”

    Try this: Pick one urge you often act on too fast, like sending a sharp text. Make a rule: wait ten minutes first.

    Dig deeper: feelings, urges and choices

Friday, 9:05am

You notice the knot in your stomach again. This time you name it: “I’m scared I’m in trouble.” You remember it’s a signal, not a verdict, and you ask your manager straight away: “Is today’s chat about something I should worry about?” “Oh no, it’s about the summer rota.” The knot loosens. The feeling was real. The story it told was not.

In everyday life

  • On your own: No one else is there to notice for you, so a daily one-word check-in with yourself matters more. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).
  • With a partner: “What are you feeling?” can sound like a test. “Do you want to tell me, or shall I just sit with you?” is easier to answer.
  • With friends: A friend going quiet may be feeling low, not cross with you. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • Parents and children: Children learn feeling words from us. Naming your own (“I’m frustrated, so I’m taking a breath”) teaches more than any lesson. See For parents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/parents).
  • At work: Feelings don’t stay at home. A short “I’m a bit flat today, not upset with anyone” can stop a team guessing. See At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).
  • If you show love by doing: Fixing, driving, cooking and turning up are love. If someone close shows care that way, you can thank them for it in words: “I noticed you cleared the drive. Thank you.”
  • With strangers: The rude person in the queue may be scared, in pain or grieving. You can’t know. You can choose not to catch it.

Common mix-ups

  • “Some feelings are bad.” Feelings aren’t good or bad. Some are painful, and some actions are harmful. The feeling itself is information.
  • “If I feel it, it must be true.” Feeling stupid doesn’t make you stupid. A feeling is a signal to check, not a fact.
  • “Letting it out always helps.” Shouting or hitting a pillow tends to keep anger going. Naming it, moving, or talking it through calmly helps more.
  • “Calm people don’t feel much.” Many calm people feel a lot. They have just practised letting feelings be there without acting on every one.
  • “I should be able to name it straight away.” Many people find feelings hard to name, and some find it very hard. That’s a difference, not a failing. Body words, numbers and colours count.
  • “Their face tells me what they feel.” Faces are a poor guide. People show the same feeling in different ways. Asking is kinder and more accurate than guessing.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Ask, don’t assign. “You’re angry” can feel like a label. “You seem upset. Am I reading that right?” leaves room for them to correct you.
  • Make the feeling make sense. “Of course you’re upset, that was a lot” helps more than advice. You can make sense of a feeling without agreeing with every action.
  • Offer choices. “Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?” Many people only want the second.
  • Accept other ways of saying it. Some people find words hard. A number, a text, a drawing or “I’m at a seven” is a real answer.
  • Don’t make their feeling about you. If their sadness makes you anxious, settle yourself first, so they don’t have to look after your feelings too.

Words you could use: “That sounds really hard.” “Do you want to talk, or would company help more?” “You don’t have to find the right word. A number is fine.”

When to get more help

Everyone has hard days and big feelings. It may be time to talk to a doctor, a counsellor or another trained professional if:

  • a low, numb, anxious or angry feeling stays most days for two weeks or more;
  • feelings are stopping you from sleeping, eating, working or seeing people;
  • you are using alcohol, drugs or other things to stop feeling;
  • you feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself. If that’s happening now, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line straight away. You deserve help today.

If you feel afraid of someone you live with or are close to, that fear is an important signal. It is not something to “manage” on your own. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy. It can’t know your situation.

Tools and reading on the website

  • Today’s Weather (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks): a short, private daily check of your mood and state.
  • Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now): steps for when a feeling is very big, very fast.
  • The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11): a plan, made on a calm day, for heated moments.
  • Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself): how you tend to feel and react, and why.
  • The library: what emotions are (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions), naming feelings, emotional granularity, when feelings are hard to name, emotional contagion and sensing your body (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress).

More for your situation

  • Next in Part Three: Stress and the nervous system (page 209)
  • Part One, Now: your wiring, your weather and your words (page 39)
  • Wired differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently) and Neurodivergent relationships (spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships)
  • For teens: when feelings get loud (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens)
  • For caregivers: resentment and guilt (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers)
  • Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief)
  • Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship): find the pages for your situation.

What to remember

  • A feeling is a signal, not a verdict. It says “something here matters to me.” It doesn’t say what to do.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often comes before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • Feeling it isn’t doing it. You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Part Three · Chapter 2

Stress and the nervous system: the ladder, flooding, rest and recovery

What stress does to your body and your mind, why kind people say things they don’t mean when they are flooded, and the kinds of rest that actually help you recover.

In this chapter

  1. Stress is your body getting ready
  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it
  3. The ladder: three everyday states
  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline
  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling
  6. Settle the body first
  7. Rest isn’t one thing
  8. Sleep and stress feed each other
  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short:

  • Stress is your body getting ready for a demand. A little helps. Too much, for too long, wears you down.
  • Three everyday states: calm and connected, revved up, and running on empty. Each one changes how you think and hear.
  • Flooded means offline. When stress is very high, listening and careful thinking get much harder. Pause, settle, then come back.
  • Rest is a skill. Different kinds of tired need different kinds of rest.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • How much are you carrying? and the stress tank (Part Two, Chapter III (page 132)) work because stress adds up from many small loads. A full tank makes small things feel big, so you check the tank before you judge the moment. Big idea: read your state first.
  • The Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now (page 39)) settles the body before any words, because a flooded body can’t think or listen. Its “come back at a set time” rule stops a pause looking like walking out.
  • The setup score (Part Two, Chapter II (page 110)) counts stress as well as hours, because a split that looks fair on paper can still leave one person running on empty.

Monday, 7:52am

The bus is late, the kids can’t find a shoe, and your phone buzzes with a work message. Your partner says, “Have you seen my keys?” and you hear yourself snap, “I’m not your secretary!” A second later you think, “Where did that come from?” It came from a body that was already full.

The last chapter looked at feelings. This one looks at the system underneath them: your nervous system, and what happens to it under pressure. Understanding stress won’t make life less busy. It can make your reactions, and other people’s, a lot less mysterious.

  1. Stress is your body getting ready.

    When something needs dealing with, your body gears up: the heart speeds, breathing quickens, muscles tense and stress hormones rise. This is useful. It helps you catch a falling glass, meet a deadline or speak up. The trouble starts when the body stays geared up for too long, with no chance to come back down.

    For example: A nurse handles an emergency calmly and well. Two hours later, at home, she can’t sit still and cries at an advert. Her body is still running the emergency.

    Thoughts you could try: “My body is getting ready for something. That’s its job.” “The emergency is over. I can let my body catch up.”

    Try this: After something stressful, give your body a clear “it’s over” signal: a walk, a shower, a stretch or a song.

    Dig deeper: the stress response

  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it.

    The same event can be easy for one person and huge for another. Stress grows when a demand looks bigger than what you have to meet it: time, energy, money, help, skills or sleep. That’s why a small thing can tip you over on a bad day, and why giving someone more support can shrink their stress without changing the task at all.

    For example: Two coworkers get the same tight deadline. One has a quiet evening ahead. The other has a sick child at home. Same task. Very different stress.

    Words you could use: “It’s not the task, it’s that I don’t have much left today.” “What would make this feel more doable?”

    Try this: When something feels huge, write two lists: what it asks of you, and what you have. Then ask what could make the second list longer.

    Dig deeper: demands and resources

  3. The ladder: three everyday states.

    The ladder is a picture, not a real ladder. In plain words, it means three states your body moves between during the day. This book uses three plain words for them. Calm and connected: breathing is easy and you can hear hard things. Revved up: fast, tense, and small things feel urgent or personal. Running on empty: flat, slow and short of words.

    You move up and down all day. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is a thirty-second self-check. It gives a best guess, not a reading.

    For example: A grandfather minding a toddler all afternoon is calm at two, revved up by four and running on empty by six. The same toddler, the same grandfather. The state changed.

    Words you could use: “I’m revved up right now.” “I’m running on empty. Can this wait till morning?”

    Try this: Set three reminders today. Each time, pick a rung: calm, revved up or running on empty. No judging, just noticing.

    Dig deeper: the ladder

  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline.

    At the top of the stress curve, the body is in full alarm. Careful thinking, listening and seeing the other side get much harder. Many people call this being flooded. You might say things you don’t mean, freeze, or only want to get away. It isn’t a character flaw. It’s a body that needs to come down before the talk can go on.

    For example: Two adult siblings start sorting their late father’s things. Within minutes they are shouting about a lamp. Neither cares about the lamp. Both are flooded with grief.

    Words you could use: “I’m too flooded to listen well. Can we stop for twenty minutes and come back at four?”

    Try this: Learn your own flood signs: heat, a racing heart, tunnel vision, a loud inner voice. When you notice two of them, pause.

    Dig deeper: flooding

  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling.

    Think of a tank (in plain words: how much stress you are already carrying today). Stress from one place spills into the next. Traffic, a hard meeting, a noisy shop and a worrying text can all fill the same tank. By evening, a tiny thing makes it overflow. The last drop gets the blame, but the tank was nearly full already. Small daily hassles count, not just big events.

    For example: A teenager explodes when asked to empty the dishwasher. The dishwasher isn’t the problem. A friendship fell apart at lunch, and the dishwasher was the last drop.

    Words you could use: “My tank was already full when I got home. That wasn’t really about you.” “Rough day? You don’t have to explain.”

    Try this: Before reacting to a small thing in the evening, ask: “How full was I before this happened?” Part Two’s Chapter III (page 132) has a simple way to tell.

    Dig deeper: why stress adds up

    Professor Puddles

    Stress fills up a little at a time, like a puddle in a long shower of rain. I would know. Five quick questions tell you how full yours is today.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  6. Settle the body first.

    You can’t think your way out of a body in alarm. You can help the body come down, and the thinking often follows. Slow breathing with long out-breaths, moving, cold water on your face, a familiar song, pressure (like a heavy blanket) or simply leaving a noisy room can all help. Different things work for different people.

    For example: A manager feels her heart race before giving hard feedback. She walks round the block once, breathing out slowly. She goes in steadier.

    Thoughts you could try: “Body first, words second.” “What has helped me settle before?”

    Try this: On a calm day, list three things that settle you. Keep the list on your phone. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) helps you build it.

    Dig deeper: settling the body

  7. Rest isn’t one thing.

    Lying on the sofa scrolling isn’t always rest. Recovery comes in different kinds: sleep, switching off from work in your head, real relaxation, doing something absorbing you enjoy, and feeling in charge of your own time. Different kinds of tired need different kinds of rest. Being with people restores some people and drains others.

    For example: Housemates plan a “relaxing” Saturday party. One loves it and wakes up refreshed. The other needs all of Sunday alone to recover. Both rested. They just needed different things.

    Words you could use: “I need quiet rest tonight, not people rest. It’s not about you.” “What kind of tired are you?”

    Try this: Ask yourself: am I body-tired, people-tired, brain-tired or feelings-tired? Pick a rest that matches.

    Dig deeper: kinds of rest

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: rest can be a nap, a walk or ten minutes of soft music. Find the kind that suits you, and keep it close.

    Tool: Calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  8. Sleep and stress feed each other.

    Stress makes sleep harder, and poor sleep makes stress hit harder. After a short or broken night, small things feel bigger, tempers are shorter and people pull away from each other. In a brain-scan study by Yoo and colleagues (2007), one night without sleep made the brain’s alarm centre react more strongly to upsetting pictures.

    In a daily study by Gordon and Chen (2014), people reported more conflict with their partner after nights of poor sleep. And in experiments by Ben Simon and Walker (2018), people who had missed a night’s sleep kept others at a greater distance and felt lonelier. You can’t always fix sleep, but you can notice when it’s part of the story.

    For example: A nurse coming off three night shifts finds herself in tears over a parking ticket. Her sister says, “You’ve barely slept. Let’s sort it out on Thursday.” On Thursday, it’s just a parking ticket.

    Words you could use: “I slept badly. If I’m short with you today, that’s why, and it’s not about you.” “Can we talk about this after we’ve both slept?”

    Try this: Before a hard conversation, ask: “Have we both slept?” If not, pick another time. At night, try the same few calm steps before bed, in the same order, so your body learns the signal. If poor sleep goes on for weeks, talk to a doctor. Sleep problems are common and often treatable.

    Dig deeper: sleep and stress

  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared.

    People calm each other. A steady voice, a hand on the shoulder or just a quiet person nearby can help a nervous system settle. Saying your state out loud also helps others read you right: “I’m stressed about work” stops a partner or friend from thinking it’s about them. Sharing stress isn’t dumping it. It’s letting someone stand beside you.

    For example: A father tells his ten-year-old, “I’m a bit stressed about money this month. It’s my grown-up job to sort it, and you’re not in trouble.” His son stops tiptoeing round him.

    Words you could use: “I’m stressed, and it’s not about you.” “Do you want help, a hug, or just some space?”

    Try this: Tonight, tell one person your state in one sentence, and ask theirs.

    Dig deeper: stress between people

Monday, 7:58am

Six minutes after the snap, you find your partner by the door. “Sorry. My tank was full before you said a word. Your keys are on the bathroom shelf.” They laugh. “Rough start?” “Very.” The morning is still busy. It isn’t a fight anymore.

In everyday life

  • On your own: No one notices you’re running on empty, so build rest in before you need it. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).
  • With a partner: Agree a pause word on a calm day, and that whoever pauses names a time to come back. See One of you wants to talk now, the other needs space (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw).
  • With friends: A friend who cancels again may be overwhelmed, not uninterested. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • Parents and children: A child can’t settle until the nearest grown-up does. Your calm is borrowed before it is learned.
  • At work: A flooded colleague can’t take in feedback. Waiting an hour often works better than pushing now. See At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).
  • Shift work, illness and caring: Some people run on empty for structural reasons. That calls for a different setup, not more effort. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours), When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) and Caregivers (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers).
  • If you have ADHD: Keeping track of everything quietly fills the tank before the day starts. Move the remembering out of your head (a shared list, labelled alarms, one place for keys), and plan hard talks for your better time of day. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-2-stress-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “All stress is bad.” Short bursts of stress help you rise to a challenge. The problem is stress with no recovery.
  • “If I’m calm, I can’t be upset.” Calm means steady, not happy. You can be calm and sad, or calm and firm.
  • “Pausing is avoiding.” A pause with a time to come back is a way to finish the talk well. A pause with no return is avoiding.
  • “Rest is lazy.” Recovery is part of the work. Bodies and minds that never recover tend to break down.
  • “Everyone should be able to handle what I can.” People have different loads, different bodies and different resources. Compare the load, not the person.
  • “Running on empty means they don’t care.” Short replies and flat faces often mean tired, not cold.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Be the calm, not the coach. A lower voice, slower words and a steady presence help more than “calm down.”
  • Lighten the load, not just the mood. Taking one task off someone’s list can do more than any pep talk.
  • Ask what kind of help. Practical help, company, a distraction or space? Ask, don’t guess.
  • Don’t debate someone who is flooded. Offer a break and a time to come back. Facts can wait twenty minutes.
  • Notice long stretches. If someone has been running on empty for weeks, gently mention it, and help them find support.

Words you could use: “You seem really stretched. Is there one thing I could take off your plate?” “We don’t have to sort this now. Shall we pick it up after dinner?”

When to get more help

Stress is normal. Constant stress that never lets up is a warning sign. It may be time to see a doctor, counsellor or other trained professional if:

  • you’ve felt exhausted, dread-filled or numb most days for several weeks, even after rest;
  • you can’t sleep, or sleep but never feel rested;
  • you have physical signs that worry you, such as chest pain, constant headaches or stomach trouble (always get chest pain checked straight away);
  • you’re relying on alcohol, drugs or other habits to get through the day;
  • you feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself. If that is happening now, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line.

If the stress comes from being afraid of someone, such as how they will react, what they will do or whether you are allowed to leave, that is not ordinary stress. Your body may be warning you. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not medical advice or diagnosis.

Tools and reading on the website

  • The Nervous System Ladder: a thirty-second self-check.
  • Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now): steps to calm down, alone or together.
  • The Calm-Down Kit: your plan for heated moments.
  • Drift (spreadloveandacceptance.com/calm-visualizer), Brain Breakers (spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes) and calm games (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pause-and-play): gentle ways to come down.
  • The library: the stress response (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress), appraisal, the window of tolerance, flooding (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships), burnout and slow breathing (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/calm).

  • Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship)

What to remember

  • Stress is your body getting ready for a demand. A little helps. Too much, for too long, wears you down.
  • Three everyday states: calm and connected, revved up, and running on empty. Each one changes how you think and hear.
  • Flooded means offline. When stress is very high, listening and careful thinking get much harder. Pause, settle, then come back.
  • Rest is a skill. Different kinds of tired need different kinds of rest.
